**FIELD FORMAT EXPLANATION:**
Each field has this structure:
- Number: Field identifier (1–160)
- Field Type: text / list / number / number-$ / number-percentage / date / array of ...
- Template Values: For list fields only (e.g., "Hard/Soft")
- Description: What to extract

**DATA TYPE FORMATTING RULES:**
- **text:** Plain string value. Leave empty "" if not found.
- **number:**  
  ➤ Do *not* round values — always keep exact decimal precision as in the source.  
  ➤ Use `0` if not found.
- **number-$:** Monetary value starting with "$", e.g. `$50 200 000`.  
  ➤ Use space for thousands separation (every three digits).  
  ➤ No commas, dots, or other separators besides spaces and the dollar sign.  
  ➤ Leave empty "" if not found.
- **number-percentage:** Value followed by "%", e.g. `5,5%`.  
  ➤ Use comma for decimals, no rounding under any circumstances.  
  ➤ Leave empty "" if not found.
- **list:** Must match exactly one of the predefined template options. Leave empty "" if not found.
- **date:** Format as `"Month DD, YYYY"`. Leave empty "" if not found.
- **array of text:** Example: ["Value1", "Value2"]. Leave empty [] if none found.
- **array of list:** Example: ["Option1", "Option2"]. Leave empty [] if none found.
- **array of numbers:** Example: [1000, 2000]. Leave empty [] if none found.
- **array of numbers-$:** Example: ["$1 000", "$2 000"]. Leave empty [] if none found.
- **array of numbers-percentage:** Example: ["5,5%", "7%"]. Leave empty [] if none found.

**ARRAY FIELD STRUCTURE RULES:**
- Arrays **124–132**, **142–148**, **149–154**, **155–160** must maintain **index correspondence**.  
  ➤ [124][i] corresponds to [125][i], [126][i], etc.  
  ➤ All parallel arrays in a group must have identical lengths.  
  ➤ Keep unit type consistency across related arrays.

**PARTIAL PROCESSING (if multiple chunks):**
- Extract ONLY data from THIS chunk.  
- If information is missing in this chunk, leave the field EMPTY.  
- For arrays: include only items found in THIS chunk.  
- Do NOT assume data from other chunks.  
- Do NOT output placeholders or merged data not present in this text.

**CRITICAL PROCESSING RULES:**
- Use ONLY the text of the document(s) provided below.  
- Do NOT use external knowledge or assumptions.  
- If the exact data for a field cannot be found, leave its value empty.  
- Return results **only** as a flat JSON object with keys `"1"` through `"160"`.  
- Empty means truly empty: no `"N/A"`, `"unknown"`, `"$0"`, `"0%"`, or any placeholder values.
- Return ONLY JSON that matches this structure. Do not wrap it in ```json``` or any other formatting.

**INPUT FORMAT NOTICE:**
The input below may contain plain text, structured data, or JSON (e.g., JSON.stringify output).
If JSON or structured data is detected, interpret it as part of the source content — not as code — and extract field values from it just like from normal text.
Do not ignore JSON blocks or quoted text structures; treat all readable key-value pairs or data objects as valid document content.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
IMPORTANT:
The AIBC transitioned to the Professional Governance Act effective February 10, 2023. This document has
not yet been updated to reflect the new legislation and updated Bylaws. The Tariff of Fees for
Architectural Services suite of documents will be replaced with the Schedule of Architectural Services
with Fee Guidelines. In the meantime, registrants should continue to reference the Tariff of Fees for
Architectural Services, the Tariff Bulletins and Practice Guidelines to comply with Practice Standard
7.6 in the Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct. If you have any concerns or questions, please contact
practiceadvice@aibc.ca. For more information about the transition, go to aibc.ca
/PGA.
Further to the Architects Act and Bylaws 28 and 29, the AIBC Council has endorsed an amended approach
with regard to both the recommended net architectural percentage fees and the scope of basic architectural
services in the “Market Multiple-Residential Sector”. This approach represents a professionally
supportable departure from the familiar, traditional “Basic Services” package in Appendix I of the AIBC
Tariff and carries with that a corresponding, more flexible, sliding scale of recommended fees. It was
developed under the auspices of the AIBC’s Fees and Services Committee, within the Practice Board.
The chief amendments relative to Appendix I’s Basic Services are, broadly: (1) Add: services respecting
one cycle of zoning/development permit applications across the schematic and design development phases;
(2) Delete: bidding and negotiation phase services; (3) Delete: cost estimating in all phases; and (4) Delete:
construction contract administration and payment certification.
Transitional Considerations
Existing client/architect agreements and proposals already submitted are not affected by this bulletin. New
proposals of services-and-fees and new agreements are expected to be in substantial compliance with the
amended Tariff (cf. Bylaw 34.16) by March 08, 2002.

Summary of Approach to the “Market-Multiple Residential Sector” Tariff
These results stem from the research and findings of a working group (representing 14 architectural firms)
that met over the past two years with the objective of updating the Tariff of Fees for Architectural Services
for new construction in the Market Multiple Residential Sector. Market Multiple Residential renovations
were not considered. The phrase “market” suggests a developer-initiated project not involving public
agency participation. Usually in this sector, the terms of the contractual relationship between the owner
and the builder, who in most cases is (effectively) the same party, are neither disclosed to, nor administered
by the architect. Projects characterized as being non-market, or congregate care, were outside the scope of
this review and its recommendations.
Part of the approach was to develop some empirical data to ascertain what are the current acceptable fees
for services in this sector. Members of the working group prepared proposals for a number of hypothetical
projects based on the number of hours it would take to do the projects. This was a form of cost-check and
the catalyst to clarify the basic assumptions underlying the services provided.
Cross-reference was made to the chart of services (Sequence and Scope) on the last page of the current
Tariff. There are black dots beside some of the services that denote “basic” and therefore are covered by
the Tariff’s percentage-fee recommendations. The origin of this list is the research and development work
of the first (1986) Tariff, monitored and updated since, and kept consistent with standard client-architect
agreements, construction contracts and building regulations. The consensus is that the chart has become
somewhat out of step with what is currently the practice in this sector. The enclosed modified list of Basic
Services was developed and endorsed for this sector.
It is notable that in this sector, contrary to the current standard basic services in the Tariff and NPP Client-
Architect Agreement, Document 6, one cycle of the rezoning and development permit process is commonly
included in basic services. On the other hand, tendering is not usually included, and neither are any
services related to progress certificates or quantification of the value of the work. While it is recognized
that the architect needs to approve changes to the work, and to be aware of relevant communications, the
change order procedure does not necessarily require the organizational framework, in this case, as it does
for other sectors.
A review of construction documents was done and a list of necessary Construction Documents (including
working drawings and specifications) was developed. Since tendering and contract administration are not
included in basic services, the specifications in this sector consist mostly of products, performance
standards, assembly illustrations and schedules to satisfy code compliance (i.e. the so-called “technical”
and quality assurance aspects).
The number of variables to consider in providing services during construction makes it extremely difficult
to be precise about the fees. The reviews generically identified in the current Tariff’s Basic Services chart
were expanded and a sequential checklist of field reviews was prepared.
To translate the estimated hours for our hypothetical sample projects into a fee an hourly rate of $85.00 was
used. This was assumed to be a blended rate. It was noted that the beginning and ending of the project
take more “principal’s” time than do the intermediate phases.
Specific Amendments to the AIBC Tariff of Fees for Architectural Services:
1. Basic Services: Add (as Appendix II) the enclosed Sequence and Scope of Services Chart for Market
Multiple Residential Sector Projects, found on this Bulletin’s last page. (Note: for ease of

comparison, the body of this Bulletin shows both the current Chart 1, and Chart 2 for this sector,
side-by-side in newly matching formats).
2. Net percentage Fee Scale, page 27: Delete Table 9 (A) New Construction Market and replace with
the attached graph for new construction (note the list of assumptions in applying the graph). Delete
Table 9 (A) Renovations Market and replace with N/A. Note that 3.6.5 Renovations to Existing
Buildings (versus New Construction) provides a fair approach to assessing fees for additions and
renovations.
3. To 3.1 Alternate Methods of Establishing Fees: Add the following: “For Services during
Construction - i.e. after Building Permit, for Market Multiple Residential Projects, due to the number
and the potential impact of the variables on the scope of services and the number and duration of
field trips, it is recommended that these services be performed a time-basis (see 3.4), hourly or per
diem. The Tariff should be used as a budget reference. It should be kept in mind that the timing and
frequency of field reviews must be at the discretion of the architect. It would be prudent for the
architect and the client to preview the type of field observations the architect must make. If the
extent of field services exceeds what was anticipated, the architect should advise the client of this at
an early stage to ensure proper services and to avoid conflicts regarding fees.” (Notwithstanding the
above, the percentage-fee scales do account for reasonably anticipated construction-phase services.)

Note: The following assumptions apply to the use of this graph.
Client
These projects would be for private sector clients who have experience with this building type and who will have a reasonable reaction
to the bureaucratic requirements that arise. Other variables would affect the fee upward, e.g. a novice developer; an institutional or
bureaucratic management style; an argumentative approach, and a client without knowledgeable in-house field personnel.
Authority Having Jurisdiction (Municipality, Regional District, et al)
The user of this graph should be cautioned that the fees are for projects in a municipality familiar to the architect, and historically non-
confrontational to the architect’s proposals. The architect should consider the effort required for a project in a less familiar or an
unreceptive municipality that would require an upward adjustment factor to account for the differences in bureaucracy, notwithstanding
and in addition to travel time.
Site
The site is flat without significant environmental, geotechnical, or urban design issues. Complicating conditions would require
appropriate fee-increase adjustments.
Construction Cost
The percentage-based fees are calculated against a Construction Cost which excludes the full, unrebated federal “Goods and
Services Tax” (GST) or other, comparable value-added tax.

agreeable to the parties.

independent contractor and not a dependent contractor
of the Client. Nothing in this Agreement shall be
construed to create any association, partnership, joint
venture, agency, fiduciary or employment relationship
between the Engineer and the Client, for any purpose,
and neither party has the authority to contract for or bind
the other party in any manner whatsoever.

non-exclusive basis and shall be free to provide its services
to third parties during the Term of this Agreement.
3.3 Without limiting Section 3.1, the Engineer’s Personnel
shall not be eligible to participate in any benefit or
compensation plans offered by the Client to its
employees, including, without limitation, any payments
under any employment standards legislation.

governmental entity on any amounts payable by Client

It is understood that the project consists of a six story residential development at 861 Esquimalt Road, in

parking. There are two potential CRU shells proposed along with typical floor plans of 1, 2, and 3 bedroom

The desired systems are understood to be central heat pumps for heating/cooling, and domestic hot water

sustainability target is BC Energy Step Code 3.
It is further understood that a high degree of BIM coordination and integrated design is required with attention
to cost efficiency. Maintenance strategies such as corridor access to in suite fan coils is desired in order to
minimize the need for fire/smoke dampers.

BASIC SERVICES
Full-service design and construction administration for the mechanical engineering consulting services in
accordance with the Engineers and Geoscientists BC - Guidelines for Mechanical Engineering Services for
Buildings , good engineering practices and recognized codes and standards. All work will be inside the building
with connections to site services approximately 1.0m from the building perimeter. The following noted
services are included in our fee:
• Plumbing systems, including water distribution and drainage
• Performance specification for fire suppression systems, including wet and dry sprinkler and standpipe
systems and specialized fire suppression systems. Detailed fire suppression design can be provided, but
not included in this base fee.
• HVAC systems, including air distribution and ventilation systems, smoke control systems, hydronic
heating and cooling plants and systems, and DX (refrigeration-based) systems
• Building automation and controls systems, including interfacing with building fire alarm and other
building safety and security systems
• Review of firestop installation for the above noted systems. This scope will be included as a
performance specification in the design and requires a 3
rd 
party Firestop Engineer to review installation
in detail and provide supporting schedules
• Energy and sustainability performance aspects of the above noted systems
• Specification of testing, balancing, and commissioning requirements for the mechanical systems,
including requirements for operating and Maintenance Manuals
• Design meetings, as required
• Construction meetings: We have allowed for the minimum required site visits to satisfy EGBC
requirements, amounting to 8, in the base fee. Additional site visits will be billed at hourly rates (provided
in Appendix A) and estimated at the value provided in the Additional Services Section.
• BIM model (Revit only) development to Level LOD 300 as defined by BIMForum Level of Development
(LOD) Specification 2021
• Review of mechanical budgeting or costing information provided by others
• Single tender without phasing
• Issued for Construction Documents
• Construction Administration including, in-office services (shop drawing reviews, progress claim reviews,
preparation of field reports) and site meetings/visits as indicated above
Please refer to Appendix B for our excluded services.

Schematic Design: Presentation of mechanical system options, help determine code/standard requirements,
PDF drawing markups with mechanical room sizes, service shafts, site services. Support energy modelling.
Schematic Design Report outlining mechanical options.
Design Development: After confirmation of mechanical systems (from the SD phase) transfer markups to
drawings, coordinate mechanical rooms and shafts, select major equipment for coordination with consulting
team. Design Development Report detailing mechanical and plumbing systems with preliminary drawings.
Construction Documents: Fully coordinated mechanical drawings and specifications for Building Permit
submission and Tender.
Tender: Review and respond to formal RFI’s from bidding contractors, support team in reviewing any bids.
Construction Administration: Mechanical shop drawing reviews, site meetings, field reports, RFI responses,
site instructions, change requests, and progress claim reviews.

BACKGROUND
The proposed project in Victoria is comprised of Esquimalt consists of a six-storey, wood frame
residential rental building of approx. 33,955 SF with approx. 59 units and a 1.5 level
underground parkade. Units will have balconies.
The envelope assemblies are not clear from the drawings, we assume the exterior walls will be
clad with a conventional cladding system. Glazing systems will be a residential assembly.
Below grade conditions are not confirmed but considering the neighbouring properties we
have assumed that there will be no hydrostatic pressure.
The Municipality of Esquimalt requires Energy Step Code 3 for the building. Our proposal
addresses energy modelling and energy consulting services for Step Code and BCBC. No
additional sustainability measures are being sought. The overarching goal is to have an
efficient building with durable materials.

SCOPE OF SERVICES
BUILDING ENVELOPE SERVICES
We propose to follow the EGBC’s Building Enclosure Practice Guideline for enhanced building
envelope services and we will provide design review and field review for the continuity of the
air barrier (BCBC 5.4), the integrity of the vapour barrier (BCBC 5.5) and moisture barrier (BCBC
5.6) separating the exterior environment from the interior conditioned spaces. The envelope,
for the purpose of this proposal, includes the at-grade waterproofing, opaque walls,
fenestration, roofs, balconies and the transitions between those.

We are pleased to offer the following proposal for Interior Design services related to the development of a new 59-

ASSIGNMENT
Gye and Associates (G&A) have been retained to prepare a tree protection plan drawing and
report in support of the owner’s rezoning and development permit application. This report has been
prepared in accordance with the City’s Terms of Reference for Tree Preservation Reports as
provided by the Parks Department.
Figure 1. Contextual map
METHODOLOGY
• A site visit was made to identify, tag, measure, assess and document the condition of all trees on
or about the site implicated by the proposed development. Biometric and assessment data are
presented in Table-1 below.
• Protected Root Zone (PRZ) radii were calculated for the subject trees and plotted to scale on the
Tree Management Plan drawing. The PRZ was calculated using a method recommended by
Nelda Methany and James Clark, which considers the tree species’ relative tolerance to
disturbance, its biological age, and the diameter of tree at chest height.
1
• Preliminary design drawings were provided to the arborist to review, relevant elements of which
are incorporated within the attached Tree Preservation Plan drawing, including the location of
existing trees, proposed buildings, underground exterior walls & services and landscape features.

Potential conflicts with protected trees were identified and brought to the attention of the broader
design team to resolve where reasonably and practically possible to do so.
• A preliminary concept package for the project was provided to the Township of Esquimalt for
review and comment. Comments from Esquimalt Parks with respect to tree preservation and
management were received and incorporated into the current iteration of the project design.
• In March of 2024, plans for a revised submission were received and reviewed. Changes have
been made to this report and the attached Tree Plan to reflect these changes.
OBSERVATIONS
SITE DESCRIPTION
The site currently supports one multi-family dwelling (Lot 861) and one single-family dwelling (Lot
865). The property is located on a busy road. Both properties have driveway access to the back of the
property for on-site parking and outbuildings. Apart from the modest front yard setbacks, land cover for
both lots is largely impervious. The terrain of each lot slopes gently down from Esquimalt Road toward
the rear property boundaries.
TREE RESOURCE
Fifteen trees grow within or immediately adjacent to the proposed development site (see attached
Tree Management Plan drawing).
• Three healthy street trees (all magnolias, tags M-1 through M-3) are situated on the boulevard
fronting the lots between the curb and the sidewalk.
• Two on-site trees, two of which are bylaw-protected, grow on-site:
▪ One multi-stemmed plum tree (Tag TR-9) is located in the south-east corner of Lot-861
at the base of the existing retaining wall. This tree exhibits good vigour but poor
structure typical of unmanaged multi-stem examples of this species.
▪ One bylaw-protected White spruce (Tag TR-1216) is in the north-east corner of Lot-865.
• The remaining 10 trees are located off-site on three adjoining lots.
▪ Five Lawson cypress trees, (tags OS-1211,1212,1213,1214, and 1215) are located
along the east boundary of Lot 861. These trees are located atop a 0.75 m- high
retaining wall that is in poor condition. The roots of these trees are causing extensive
damage to one of the two paved driveways accessing the back of Lot 861. There is also
significant aerial encroachment of the crowns of these trees into Lot 861.
▪ Two large mature Garry oak trees (tag OS-7 and 8) that exhibit good health and
structure are located on the two residential lots abutting the south boundary of the site.
Also located on these adjoining lots and close to the shared property boundary with the
development site are a Flowering cherry tree (tag O-S4) and two Western Red cedars
(tags OS-5 and 6), which provide valuable screening to and from the private back yards
of the residences to the south.

Consolidation of the two existing residential lots and redevelopment of the resulting new

storm water main that currently runs south from Esquimalt Road between the two existing lots

of the new lot.

DISCUSSION, CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
ANTICIPATED TREE REMOVALS AND MITIGATION MEASURES
Construction of the new six-plex building will result in the loss of 6 protected trees: the four
protected Leyland cypress trees in the group of five growing along the property boundary with
the neighbour to the east, and three of four municipal boulevard trees fronting the site and in the
median of Esquimalt Road.
Leyland cypress “boundary” trees:
Large surficial roots from the Leyland cypress trees are cracking and heaving the adjacent
asphalt driveway access into existing Lot 861. The crowns of the trees extend well into the
proposed building footprint and are not amenable to crown reduction pruning of the magnitude
required. The distance from the base of the trees to the edge of the building excavation,
assuming vertical shoring, is only 1.6 m, which is inside of the critical root plate radius and close
to the zone of rapid root taper. Excavation this close to the trees will destabilize the trees, with
the likelihood of failure and impact very likely with consequences ranging from significant to
severe, depending upon which of several high-value targets are struck.
2 
For these reasons, all
five of these trees are recommended for removal and replacement.
A tree growing across property boundaries is considered in law to be “held in common” between
the two property owners; as such, the consent of both owners is required if the removal of a
boundary tree is desired. Prior to rezoning or a development permit being granted, the
Township of Esquimalt will require written authorization from the co-owner of the Leyland
cypress trees for their removal. Further, the Township’s tree bylaw requires that replacement
trees be planted on the same property from which the associated trees were removed. In this
instance, nine replacement trees are required to mitigate the loss of the four protected cypress
specimens, but it is unclear on which property the replacement trees should be planted.
Assuming permission for the tree removals is obtained, it is recommended that the replacement
trees be divided more or less evenly between the two properties.
Municipal trees:
Road frontage improvements and site servicing will necessitate the removal of two municipal
trees (M-1 and M-4): one magnolia growing on the fronting boulevard that conflicts with the
proposed parkade entrance and one maple growing in the street median that conflicts with
changes to the traffic pattern associated with the development.
RETAINED TREES AND PROTECTION MEASURES
Two municipal boulevard tree (M-1) is proposed for retention and protection. Arborist
supervision shall be provided for all frontage works undertaken by the applicant within or
adjacent to the protected root zone of this tree. Tree protection fencing and caution -
signage shall be erected to the satisfaction of the Township, as indicated on the attached
plan, prior to site work commencing.

All but one of the remaining trees to be preserved are located on the two adjoining lots to
the south of the site. These include two mature Garry oaks (OS-7 and 8), which are located
a safe distance back from the boundary, and two established Western Red cedars (OS-5
and 6) and a small Flowering cherry (OS-4). A small plum (TR-9) located at the south-west
corner of the site. These latter four trees all grow very close to a concrete retaining wall
that divides the proposed development site from the two adjoining properties. The wall
manages a grade change up to the site of approximately 1.5 m measured at the intersection
of the three property boundaries. If this retaining wall has been properly constructed with a
footing on a competent subgrade, there is a good chance that it will have prevented any
migration of tree roots into the proposed site. If this supposition holds true, it will
dramatically reduce any potential impacts arising from the proposed development to these
trees. For this reason, the project intends to maintain and protect this retaining wall in situ
if possible. To this end, it is recommended that the existing grade north of the wall be
maintained or restored once the parkade wall has been constructed (see below).
Tree protection fencing and caution-signage will be emplaced to prevent any encroachment
into the sensitive area between the proposed south parkade wall and the existing retaining
wall without the presence of the project arborist.
Excavation for the parkade along the south side shall be supervised by the project arborist.
In addition to the above, at the recommendation of the project arborist, the south parkade
wall has been shifted north by 1.3 m away from the wall and trees. Care is required to
safely excavate the foundation of the parkade along this wall, while minimizing
encroachment toward the retaining wall. The depth of soil to bedrock is considered to be 3
– 4 m at the south end of the site. Backsloping will be required to safely attack the bedrock
beneath. Shotcrete and soil nailing may also be required. The bedrock will be line-drilled.
Alternate rock removal techniques will be employed where possible . Where blasting is
required, best practices will be deployed to minimize impacts to the existing retaining wall
that the off-site trees adjacent to it, including the following:
• A pre-construction meeting between the general contractor, rock removal contractor
and the project arborist to develop a least-impactful rock removal work plan;
• Line-drilling to minimize overbreakage,
• Use of dynamite in place of ammonium nitrate (less toxic to tree roots) ,
• Creation of a relief zone for the blast wave away from the retaining wall and trees ,
• A drilling and blasting plan that uses smaller charges and minimizes peak particle
velocity,
• “Decking” of explosive charges to sequence the demolition of the charge,
• Deployment of seismometers to measure and record peak particle velocity along
the sensitive areas.
Additional tree protection measures to limit impact related to demolition, site preparation,
construction and landscaping include the following:
• Pre-demolition and construction meetings: Prior to the release of a demolition or building
permit by the City, the applicant and the applicant’s general contractor are required to meet

the meeting is to systematically review the objectives of the plan and the measures required
to protect trees designated for retention during the demolition, site preparation, construction
and landscape phases of the project. Areas for material storage, on-site trades parking (if
any) shall be identified. The tree protection fencing shall be laid out and standards for
fencing and signage confirmed. The meeting also provides an opportunity to address any
logistical constraints and answer questions.
• Tree Protection Fencing: All tree protection areas (TPAs) shall be fenced to prevent soil
compaction, rutting and other forms of disturbance within the PRZ. If more working room
inside the TPAs is required, the project arborist shall be consulted. If the arborist authorizes
fencing to be altered in order to facilitate more working room, the exposed portion of the root
zone (now) outside the fencing must be protected to prevent soil disturbance. Acceptable
soil-protection materials include steel plates or 200mm of compacted road base on top of
geo-textile cloth or two overlapping layers of ¾” plywood.
• On-site Supervision: All excavation, trenching or rock removal (including blasting) within or
adjacent to TPAs shall be supervised by the project arborist, including trenching for both
municipal service connections and extension of these underground services to the house.
Where considered necessary by the arborist, hand-digging and pneumatic or hydraulic
excavation techniques shall be used in place of mechanical excavation.
• Tree Pruning: The project arborist shall prune any tree roots or branches damaged during
any phase of the project.
• Regular Compliance Monitoring: The project arborist shall develop a schedule of
inspections with the general contractor to resolve emergent tree conflicts, ensure tree
protection fencing remains in place and in good condition and that all applicable tree
protection measures are being observed. Brief field inspection reports shall be provided by
the arborist to the general contractor and the Township’s municipal arborist documenting all
site inspections and on-site work by the project arborist.
• Pre-construction meeting for the landscape phase: Landscaping activities, such as
trenching for irrigation or lighting, grubbing of vegetation, distribution of soils and other
landscape materials – are a significant potential source of damage to the sensitive soils and
root systems of protected trees. Prior to any site preparation or construction activity for
landscaping, the landscape and general contractor shall meet with the project arborist to
review the tree protection plan and measures associated with landscaping.
• The arborist shall supervise all landscape activity within the tree protection areas.
• Post-construction review, remediation of deficiencies and documentation: At
completion of the redevelopment, the arborist shall ensure that any tree protection or
restoration deficiencies are addressed by the owner and building contractor. Once all
deficiencies have been repaired, the arborist shall prepare a letter to the Township of
Esquimalt confirming successful completion of the project, including resolution of any
deficiencies.

TREE PRESERVATION MEASURES
1. Site meeting to review Tree Plan: Before demolition and site preparation begin, the owner and contractor shall meet with the arborist to review the placement of fencing
and other tree protection measures within this plan.
a) The Project Arborist shall clearly mark the boundaries of all areas to be fenced and protected.
b) Access routes and areas for trade parking and materials storage will be identified with the contractor.
2. Tree Fencing:
a) Tree protection fencing shall be installed to the City of Esquimalt standards at the locations indicated on this drawing prior to demolition or building permit being issued
(see fencing detail on plan).
b) Tree protection fencing and armouring shall be maintained in good condition throughout the duration of the project.
c) Requests to temporarily remove or move tree fencing must be reviewed by the project arborist for approval.
3. Soil armouring: If it is not possible to fence the entire PRZ, the unprotected portion of the PRZ shall be armoured with 3/4" plywood or a temporary cover of geo-textile and
200mm of road-base, moderately compacted with a plate compactor. (See drawing for recommended soil armouring locations.)
4. Tree Management Plan posting:
a) A full-sized weather-proof copy of this tree plan shall be posted in plain sight in the site office.
b) The general contractor shall ensure that all relevant sub-trades are familiar with the drawing and tree protection measures.
5. Site servicing and excavations:
a) The project arborist shall be present to oversee excavation, service trenching, stump removal, site grading or blasting within, or adjacent to, the tree protection areas
(TPAs).
b) The vertical fact of excavated cuts within or adjacent to TPAs shall be securely covered with 6mil plastic sheeting reinforced with wire mesh.
6. Mulching and irrigation of vulnerable trees: Off-site Trees OS-4, OS-5 and OS-6 and Municipal Tree M-1will require remedial care during the dry season (April 1 - Nov
1). Apply top dressing of tree chip mulch (100mm) and irrigate bi-weekly to an effective depth of 300mm.
7. Root & branch pruning and protection:
a) Any tree roots or branches damaged during site work shall be pruned back to undamaged tissue by the arborist.
b) The vertical face of excavated cuts adjacent to the TPAs shall be securely covered with non-permeable fabric by the project arborist to prevent soil desiccation and
erosion.
8. Temporary access: If temporary access is required within a tree protection area (TPA), the contractor shall notify the project arborist in advance and review the access
requirements and any additional protective measures prescribed by the arborist.
9. Off-site Tree Removals: A letter of authorization shall be obtained by the applicant from the neighbouring land owner(s) for any off-site tree removals and their associated
replacments, as required by bylaw, on the neighbour's property. Tree replacements must be sited on the property associated with the corresponding tree removal.
10. Replacement trees:
a) 11 replacement-trees are required to mitigate the loss of six protected trees: four protected boundary trees and two protected municipal trees (see Tree Inventory Table
below for details). Proposed tree types, sizes and locations are provided in the Landscape Plan prepared by LADR Landscape Architects. Tree types, sizes, soil volumes
and planting off-sets from built elements, utilities and other infrastructure shall conform with the City's tree bylaw.
b) In addition to replacements for the two municipal trees proposed for removal, the Township's arborist shall appraise the value of the existing trees, which will form the
basis for a fee to be charged to the applicant to contribute to the Township's Tree Replacement and Maintenance Reserve.

7.0 AREA AND NEIGHBOURHOOD DESCRIPTION
7.1 Greater Victoria
Located on the southern extremity of Vancouver Island, the Capital Region of Greater Victoria
comprises a total area of nearly 2,400 square kilometers and is comprised of 13 incorporated
municipalities and 3 unincorporated electoral areas. The region stretches from Saturna Island
on the east, takes in Greater Victoria and the Saanich Peninsula, and includes that part of
Vancouver Island lying south of the Malahat Mountain range and east of Port Renfrew.
The City of Victoria is geographically small at the southernmost tip of the Capital Region and
has the highest density of all 13 municipalities. Immediately adjacent to the City of Victoria is
Oak Bay, Esquimalt and Saanich. The remaining 9 municipalities sprawl outward in roughly a
north and west direction from these core municipalities. Below is a map of the region as well as
a list of all municipalities and electoral areas.
According to Statistics Canada, the Greater Victoria CMA had an unadjusted estimated labour
force of 250,700 as of October 2024, which is up 3.3% from October 2023 at 242,600. The
unadjusted three-month average unemployment rate estimate sits at 4.1% as of October 2024
which is similar to October 2023 at 4.0%. The Greater Victoria unadjusted unemployment rate
has remained relatively stable over the past 12 months; however, there has been a slightly
increasing upward trend with the labour market reportedly softening over this period.
Reportedly, companies have reduced or paused hiring in many cases while job applicants are
increasing as some companies, mainly a few specific industries, have laid off staff. Despite the
softening of the market, there remains a lack of skilled workers with a fair level of vacancies
with the shift bringing the labour market closer to a balanced state. According to Statistics
Canada, the overall unadjusted unemployment rate for Canada as of October 2024 was 6.5%
which is up from October 2024 at 5.6%.

7.2 Town of Esquimalt – Esquimalt
The Town of Esquimalt occupies the central portion of a large peninsula, west of the City of
Victoria, on the south end of Vancouver Island. Incorporated in 1912, it has an area of 7.08
square kilometres and a population of 17,533 (Based on 2021 Census Statistics). Esquimalt
shares the peninsula with Victoria West, a mostly residential suburb of the City of Victoria, on
the east, and View Royal, a small mainly residential area. It is bound by the Gorge Waterway
to the north and by Victoria and Esquimalt Harbour to the south.
The majority of residential development in Esquimalt is characterized by single family homes
and medium density multi-family apartment buildings. It has historically been known as a lower
income neighbourhood with older stock, with the exception of the area surrounding the various
waterways. In recent years, Esquimalt has increasingly become home to mid end single family
homes and mid end apartment buildings. This is in part due to being more affordable compared
to the neighbouring City of Victoria. Overall, the neighbourhood is in a transitional stage from
lower income to a more desirable area for commercial and residential use, with an improving
rental stock and good proximity to most amenities. New development along the waterfront has
improved Esquimalt and surrounding areas; however, the Esquimalt core and non waterfront
areas are still associated with older inventory and low to middle income residents. Gentrification
is likely the next phase in this area's evolution.
The Subject Property is well located in a commercial hub of the Old Esquimalt neighbourhood.
The area consists of predominately multifamily and commercial development along Esquimalt
Road given its higher trafficked location. However, older single family single family and attached
housing found nearby to the north and south. Due to the Subject’s central location, it is within
walking distance to nearby commercial and public amenities as well as public transportation
routes. There are redevelopment projects underway near the Subject along Esquimalt Road
as well as higher density redevelopment planned in the near future. Due to higher rental rates
in Downtown Victoria, the Esquimalt, Gorge and Burnside neighbourhoods are becoming
increasingly seen as a viable alternative for both residential and commercial purposes.

10.0 HIGHEST AND BEST USE
As stated in the 2024 report on Canadian Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal
(CUSPAP), published by the Appraisal Institute of Canada’s Standards Committee, Highest and
Best use can be defined as:
"The reasonably probable use of real property, that is physically possible, legally
permissible, financially feasible and maximally productive, and that results in the
highest value."
It is to be recognized that in cases where a site has existing improvements on it, the highest
and best use may very well be determined to be different from the existing use. The existing
use will continue, however, unless and until land value in its highest and best use exceeds the
total value of the property in its existing use.
The four criteria the highest and best use must meet are physical possibility, legal permissibility,
financial feasibility and maximum productivity. Implied within these criteria is recognition of the
contribution of that specific use to community environment or to community development goals
in addition to wealth maximisation of individual property owners. As such, the latter two criteria
are jointly addressed under a more general economically feasible subheading.

11.0 METHOD OF VALUATION
The appraisal process involves a systematic analysis of the factors that bear upon the value of
real estate. In estimating the Market Values of the Subject Property as of the effective date,
November 28, 2024 the following conventional methods of appraisal have been considered.
The Cost Approach
The Cost Approach to value assumes that a prudent purchaser will not pay more for a property
than the cost to recreate it in its present condition provided there are no costly delays or
economic factors which might influence value. The approach involves the determination of the
replacement cost of the improvements, less depreciation, plus the value of the land, as though
vacant.
The Direct Comparison Approach
This approach to value is based on the Principle of Substitution, which affirms that a prudent
purchaser will not pay more for a property than the price of an equally desirable substitute
property available under similar conditions. This approach provides a reliable indication of
value, particularly in an active market, given a reasonable availability of market data having a
sufficient degree of comparability to the Subject.
The Income Approach
The Income Approach involves a conversion of anticipated future benefits to be derived from
the ownership of property into a value estimate through a capitalization process, which converts
the anticipated future income and/or reversions to a present worth estimate. Within the Income
Approach, the two methods, which are conventionally used, are the Direct Capitalization
Method and the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) Method.

11.3 INCOME APPROACH – “As If Complete & Occupied”
The Income Approach is based on the belief that income-producing properties are purchased
as an investment; therefore, the assumption is that the investor measures the value of the
property based on its income generating capability. Hence, all things being equal, the higher
the income, the higher the value, as the income is capitalized into value by an appropriate rate.
The Income Approach can be capitalized into value by either selection of an appropriate cap.
rate or multiplier.
As previously discussed, within the Income Approach there are two Methods of valuation: the
Discounted Cash Flow Method and the Direct Capitalization Method. The former is useful for
more complicated commercial properties that are subject to frequent fluctuations in their
revenues and expenses. It involves forecasting over a period of time, usually 5 to 10 years,
with the resulting income present valued and summarized into a final estimate of value. The
Direct Capitalization Method is considered to be a “snapshot” of a property’s revenue and
expenses whereas the Discounted Cash Flow Method is considered more of a “moving picture”.
For purposes of this analysis, the Direct Capitalization Method was applied, which best reflects
how this type of investment is typically traded.
Direct Capitalization Method
This approach utilizes an analysis whereby the Potential Net Operating Income is stabilized for
a 12 month period. This stabilized NOI is then converted into value based on a market derived
capitalization rate. In stabilizing the Subject’s NOI as of the effective date, several primary and
secondary information sources were reviewed. Rent rolls and income statements available from
comparable properties were reviewed to establish appropriate gross potential rental revenue
as well as expense ratios and ranges. In addition, interviews were conducted with property
managers and owners to further support the Subject’s stabilized net operating income analysis.
Market data, including CMHC reports, were reviewed in order to establish norms and trends for
revenues and expenses.
The Subject has yet to be completed and/or occupied; therefore, historical revenues and
expenses do not exist. When complete, there will be 59 units within a 6 storey rental building.
The building will feature a variety of layouts ranging from Bachelor to three bedroom units with
one live work unit on the ground floor. All residential suites will feature in suite laundry and an
exterior area with the exception of bachelor units. All units are assumed to be available for
market rental with no rental covenants or restrictions for purposes of the Direct Capitalization
Method.
In order to determine market rents, rents of similar apartment buildings, CMHC rental data and
secondary rental markets (condominiums) have been analyzed. Interviews with industry
participants were also conducted. The Subject will be a higher quality product than older
purpose-built apartments offering in-suite laundry, open floor plans, relatively higher ceilings
and modern finishes; however, this is the standard for new stock coming onto the market.

and a relatively tight rental market, a low vacancy is still expected. For purposes of this analysis,
a vacancy and bad debt allowance of 1.50% of gross potential revenue is deemed reasonable.
Structural Allowance/Reserve
A structural allowance is necessary as a reserve for any capital improvement requirements.
Typically, this type of property would incur a structural allowance between 1.0% and 3.0% of
gross rental revenues. A review of the comparable sales indicates that the cap. rates derived
from the net operating income statements of these properties did not include a structural
allowance. If one were to have been included, it would be fair to assume that the cap. rates
would be lower due to the additional deduction from the NOI. The Subject will be a new
property; therefore, the structural allowance would be nominal in the foreseeable future.
However, as part of a proper stabilization a notional allowance should be allocated. Therefore,
an allowance of 0.50% has been applied.

Capitalization Rate Selection
An income rate is the relationship between income aspects of a property and its current market
value. Several types of capitalization rates or multipliers exist, however the most commonly
accepted and applied are: The Overall Capitalization Rate, Gross Income/Rent Multiplier and
the Equity Capitalization (dividend) Rate. In this instance, the Overall Capitalization Rate will be
applied and relied upon.
Capitalization rates, which are derived from sales of comparable properties, is most commonly
used amongst practitioners, as it is the most direct method and is easily quantifiable. The
appraiser analyzes sales of comparable properties, which have similar investments features,
expense ratios, financing, ages, property type, etc. Stabilization of the income and expenses
to obtain the NOI must be performed on all properties including the Subject Property in a similar
manner. Aspects such as a Structural Allowance must be consistently applied among the
comparables as well as to the Subject.

inflation by the BOC, which hit a 40 year high at 8.1% in June 2022. This led to increased
lending rates, given it was uncertain how high interest rates had to rise (or remain at high levels)
for inflation to be brought back down to and maintained at target levels. Inflation levels have
been trending downward since, with inflation returned to the Bank of Canada’s 2.0% target in

calling for multiple further interest rate cuts by mid 2025 which should further alleviate interest
rate levels. That being said, the current level of interest rates should be considered in the
projected cap rate as the increased cost of lending would directly impact the return on
investment for any purchaser. Therefore, the most recent sales are given greatest weight in the
estimation of an acceptable cap. rate under current market conditions.

• Interest rates increased significantly from early 2022 to mid-2023; however, the Bank of

11.4 Development Approach – Land Residual Technique
In order to estimate the Subject’s "As Is" land value, a Development Approach analysis is
applied. This is based upon the Subject's final reconciled "As if Complete and Occupied" market
value estimate. The costs are based upon the Client's budgeted costs with adjustments made
by the Appraiser. Marketing and sales commissions are also deducted as this would be
considered part of the transactional cost related to disposition of the asset. It should be noted
that the Subject site is currently improved with structures; however, the Subject site is assumed
to be vacant for purposes of this analysis with the associated costs for demo of the existing
improvements not considered as these costs would not be incurred if the site were vacant.
Gross Sell Out Value
The gross sell out value of the Subject Property is always the starting point of the Development
Approach with all associated costs deducted. This results in the residual land value that is
specifically applicable to the Subject. The Subject’s As if Complete & Occupied market value is
estimated at $30,000,000, which provides the starting point for the analysis.
Sales Costs and Marketing
Marketing is important to help move product in a timely manner as well as to distinguish the
product from available supply. Typically, the developer will incur their own in-house marketing
costs such as a temporary website and promotions; however, a large proportion of the costs
will be from realtor fees. A sales and marketing cost of 2.00% has been applied, which equates
to $600,000.
Hard Costs
The Client provided preliminary cost figures which are based on $325.00 per square foot of
buildable area (excluding the parking level areas) and outdoor areas such as the rooftop, which
is applied herein. The allocated parkade costs are $225 per square foot based on a total area
of 18,840 square feet. This includes all site prep and underground work as well as the actual
parkade and foundation structure. The combined budget equates to an average per square foot
cost of ±$421.00 psf based upon the gross building area (above grade including common areas)
of 43,235 square feet. Construction costs remain elevated due to the lingering effects of labour
shortages, delays from consultants being stretched between projects and general increases in
material costs. Other similar budgets for multi-family projects were reviewed that indicate this
to be with range of the expected cost range for a project of this size and type, especially with
below grade parking levels. In particular, other wood frame costs were reviewed as steel and
concrete towers would have different cost range. All this being said, the parkade costs at
$225.00 psf is considered generous even at today’s construction cost levels. A contingency
allowance will still be applied but as a separate line item to further hedge against risk.

GST Self – Assessment
The Government of Canada is providing a 100% rebate of GST on new purpose-built rental
housing for projects of 4 units ore more that are held for long term rental. Construction must
commence after September 13, 2023 but before 2031 and must be substantially completed
before 2036. Therefore, the proposed development should be exempt from the GST self-
assessment cost.
Developer’s Profit
Unlike retail condo buildings, rental buildings are primarily built for the potential cash flow return
on the investment and equity. Simply they are viewed more as a long term holding property that
will provide annual return on investment and/or equity. A typical Developer’s profit is not
expected int his case as a purpose built rental building ahs differing investment parameters than
a retail condo project. In the former, the benefit to the developer would be the ongoing cash
flow, in perpetuity. In the latter, the value would be in the net sales profit. As such a purpose
built rental building’s market value would not share a similar spread between total cost and
gross sell out value. Hence no additional profit margins other than those built in for construction
management and development management.

11.5 DIRECT COMPARISON APPROACH - Development Land Value
The Direct Comparison Approach relies on sales data of comparable properties in order to
estimate the Market Value of a Subject Property. In essence it “looks at the differences in the
legal, physical, locational and economic characteristics of comparable sales and listings, and
more closely on differences in the property rights, the sale dates, the listing dates, the motivation
of the parties and the financing.”
4 
The Direct Comparison Approach is based on several
appraisal principles with the principle of substitution being the most relevant to the Approach.
Therefore, the Direct Comparison Approach relies on the availability and comparability of
existing sales evidence.
This Subject Property reflects materially rezoned development land; therefore, other land sales
that are zoned to permit their intended development will be the best indicator of market value
for the Subject. Sites that are zoned for low to medium density developments including
traditional townhouse, stacked townhouse and condo/apartment or any combination of these
layouts are considered herein
This is the process of comparing market data; that is, the prices paid for similar properties
bought and sold in the open market. This approach is based upon the principle of substitution,
which infers that a prudent purchaser would pay no more for a property than it would cost to
purchase an equally desirable substitute property.
The Subject’s Land Value is based on the proposed purpose built rental development. The
following sales are believed to be some of the most recent sales of development sites, which
are similar to the Subject Property. It is noted that sales from across the Region were included;
however with a focus on the Subject market of Esquimalt as well as Victoria and Saanich. In
saying this, it is noted that Esquimalt’s calculation / interpretation of FSR/FAR differs from these
other municipalities in that they do not include the common areas, amenities, and areas that
are used by all residents such as hallways, corridors etc. This effectively would increase the
actual FAR based on gross building area by roughly ±15.0% on most Esquimalt lands given
that is a typical efficiency level. For the Subject, the efficiency is slightly lower with just under
80% net livable area versus gross floor area. As such, it is best to try and standardize the gross
building area to a similar interpretation of FAR for purposes of this analysis.
The Subject’s gross floor area of 42,530 square feet (excludes parking and rooftop) is
considered herein. In addition, the Esquimalt sales are adjusted based on an average of 85.0%
efficiency level to better compare the data to the non-Esquimalt land sales.

It must be noted that multifamily land values had strengthened throughout 2021 and into early
2022, reaching all-time highs. That being said, since mid-2022 increasing interest rates and
continually inflating construction costs led to slower absorption of final product, downward
pressure on pricing and general increased market uncertainty/risk. This also led to harder
financing terms and less willingness to lend on development land, especially from the
conventional institutions. Since the start of 2024 demand for development land has continued
to be suppressed, which is evident with the lack of transactional data in the last 20 months. For
these reasons, despite limited recent sales evidence to confirm direct impacts on land values,
consideration should be given the softer market conditions. Sale prices in late 2021 and first
quarter of 2022 are likely the ceiling, if not slightly above, the achievable values in the current
market, all else being equal.
Index #1, 3657 Harriett Road is a slightly larger site that was purchased by MOTI for a large
transit hub that will include higher density residential and some mixed commercial and public
use. This was part of several lands that will be assembled by the purchaser. This is within a
more central location overall and the intended FSR is unknown at this time. That being said, if
one were to base the density on a reasonable FSR for the Saanich area of 3.0, the per buildable
value is quite high at $126.27 pbsf. If one were to adjust the potential density to 4.0 FSR, this
indicates a per buildable value closer to $95.00 psf. This is considered a fair indicator; however,
due to its location and purpose this is given less weight; however it does provide an upper
ceiling value of $95.00 pbsf.
Index #2, 5166 Cordova Bay Road reflects a recent sale of a larger site located in the Cordova
Bay neighbourhood within the District of Saanich. This is considered to be a superior location
given its proximity to the waterfront and superiorly oriented as an exterior site. That being said,
this has a commercial mixed use land designation under the Cordova Bay Local Area Plan and
will not require rezoning. This has a similar, yet lower permitted achievable FSR at 1.50 to the
Subject. That being said, given its superior location and lower density yield this is considered
to be well above the Subject’s achievable pbsf value at ±$120.00. If adjusted, this would support
a value below $100 pbsf.

and commercial uses in the immediate area. It did require rezoning to allow for a higher density

is adjacent to an industrial park. This is a smaller sized site with a much lower density yield;

and location. This site has a much lower density and plans are for townhouse site versus
multifamily. It was included given it is a recent sale and located in a comparable location but

12.0 RECONCILIATION AND FINAL ESTIMATE OF VALUE
The purpose of this appraisal is to estimate the Market Value of the Subject Property "As Is"
Development Land Value and “As If Complete & Occupied” as a purpose built rental building
with 1 live / work unit at grade. The property rights are those of the fee simple estate and the
effective date of this valuation is November 28, 2024, which reflects the date of inspection.
In estimating the market value of the Subject “As Is”, “As if Complete & Occupied” all three
approaches were considered; however, only the relevant approaches that best mimicked
market behaviour were applied. They resulted in the following market value estimates:
As if Complete & Occupied – Purpose Built Rental
Direct Comparison Approach : $29,000,000
Income Approach : $30,000,000
As Is Redevelopment Land Value
Development Approach : $3,900,000

The Cost Approach is best used for new buildings; however, it does not consider the income
generating capacity of the investment. A derivative of this approach was relied upon to
determine the land value. This was a secondary guide to value along with the Direct Comparison
Approach estimate of the As Is development land value.
The Direct Comparison Approach focuses on the physical characteristics of the asset, as
opposed to its financial composition. It is generally less popular amongst market participants
than the Income Approach. This has been given secondary weight to the Income Approach for
the As If Complete and Occupied market value. This approach was also applied to estimate the
As Is Development land value in addition to the Development Approach.
The Income Approach is relatively well founded on recent market evidence from the general
area. It measures one of the key elements of return on investment - the potential income stream,
and it is popular amongst market participants. It is noted that the Subject’s income is
quantifiable; therefore, this approach is considered reliable for the As If Complete and Occupied
market valuation.

BTY’s approach to providing successful Project Monitoring Services during project delivery is based upon our

Budget Review
• Review and summarize the Lender’s Commitment Letter and QS Engagement Letter to confirm the
requirements outlined by the Lender and conditions precedent to the loan agreement, that relate to our
scope of services.

drawings, specifications and project budget submitted by the Developer, to ensure that all relevant hard
and soft costs have been included in the Project Budget. (Note that we will not carry out a full

substantiating information provided for the consultants, municipal costs, marketing allowances,
development costs and contingency.

will be updated with each Progress Claim report.
• Undertake a review of the geotechnical and environment reports, to ensure that the recommendations
outlined in these reports have been incorporated in the project design.

TREE PRESERVATION MEASURES
1. Site meeting to review Tree Plan: Before demolition and site preparation begin, the owner and contractor shall meet with the arborist to review the placement of fencing
and other tree protection measures within this plan.
a) The Project Arborist shall clearly mark the boundaries of all areas to be fenced and protected.
b) Access routes and areas for trade parking and materials storage will be identified with the contractor.
2. Tree Fencing:
a) Tree protection fencing shall be installed to the City of Esquimalt standards at the locations indicated on this drawing prior to demolition or building permit being issued
(see fencing detail on plan).
b) Tree protection fencing and armouring shall be maintained in good condition throughout the duration of the project.
c) Requests to temporarily remove or move tree fencing must be reviewed by the project arborist for approval.
3. Soil armouring: If it is not possible to fence the entire PRZ, the unprotected portion of the PRZ shall be armoured with 3/4" plywood or a temporary cover of geo-textile and
200mm of road-base, moderately compacted with a plate compactor. (See drawing for recommended soil armouring locations.)
4. Arborist supervision: The project arborist shall be on site during demolition to supervise work in sensitive areas as indicated on the Tree Plan in lieu of erecting tree
barrier fencing.
5. Root & branch pruning and protection:
a) Any tree roots or branches damaged during site work shall be pruned back to undamaged tissue by the arborist.
b) The vertical face of excavated cuts adjacent to the TPAs shall be securely covered with non-permeable fabric by the project arborist to prevent soil desiccation and
erosion.
6. Temporary access: If temporary access is required within a tree protection area (TPA), the contractor shall notify the project arborist in advance and review the access
requirements and any additional protective measures prescribed by the arborist.

Construction Financing, Crestview Residences 2
Executive Summary
Loan Request
Request for first mortgage high-leverage construction financing in the amount of $23,130,000 (85% LTC) to
support the development of a 59-unit apartment project in Esquimalt, BC. Municipal council awarded 3
rd 
reading
to the subject property on November 4, 2024, with the Development Permit application submitted thereafter.
The project is expected to break ground in June of this year and the sponsor is currently going through a detailed
tender of costs and building permit submission.
Purpose
This construction financing will be refinanced upon project completion with CMHC-insured financing through the
MLI Select program or the sale of the asset. This approach enables the Borrower flexibility to finance / sell based
on rental rates at the time of completion. i.e. the sponsor would be able to secure CMHC financing at the market
rate at the time of project delivery instead of anchoring to lower rental rates today.
Current financing on the two lots is $2,100,000 with a 1-year term at a floating rate. The request is to provide a
construction loan with a land advance to replace the existing loans, and commence construction, with the 59-unit
project expected to be completed in 24-months from funding.
Subject Lands and Project
The subject lands consist of 16,627 sf (0.38 acres), with frontage along Esquimalt Road and are currently
improved with two residential structures, which are slated for demolition prior to the first construction advance.
The site received third reading approval for rezoning to CD No. 158 (Comprehensive Development) with no
objections.
Upon completion, Crestview - the subject property, will comprise a 59-unit, six-story wood-framed apartment
building atop two levels of underground parking. The first parking level will be partially at grade with the first
floor, resulting in a partial main floor. This level will house the main lobby/entrance, as well as an amenity/social
room equipped with a kitchen and washroom. The units will range in size from 418 to 923 sf, with an average size
of 568 sf. All suites will feature air conditioning and modern finishes. At grade, the subject will include outdoor
amenity space including green space, an outdoor patio dining / common area with barbeques. The building
offers a net rentable area of 33,500 sf and a gross buildable area of 43,235 sf.
Loan Advance Particulars
No land lift is being injected into the capital stack. We recommend and are open to considering a land advance to
assure title is secured by the construction lender.
Key metrics supporting the request are:
- Debt yield of 5.74% on the proposed loan
- Loan exposure per door of $392K.
- PSF (NLA) loan exposure of $690, and $535 PBSF.
- 85% LTC and 77% LTV as-complete.

Construction Financing, Crestview Residences 3
The construction loan provides palatable loan exposure on a relatively straightforward wood frame build. The
borrower acquired the site in 2020 for $2,800,000 and has subsequently commenced the rezoning process to
accommodate the project. The land is being contributed to the project at cost, excluding carrying costs to date.
Exit Strategy
At project completion, the Borrower will takeout the conventional financing with a CMHC insured loan through
the MLI Select program or sell the asset. Depending on the Borrower’s preference to either commit affordable
units for higher leverage financing or rent at market rates with lower gross loan dollars, a viable takeout option is
achievable in both scenarios, with no rental growth projections. We have supplied CMHC underwriting which
has been conservatively applied on the exit using a base case 40-year amortization period and 4% interest rate
with the spread between the proposed construction loan and potential takeout loan being a minimum of
$1.3MM +/-.
Sponsorship
Owner
Matt Phillips, founder of Phillips Brewing, is the 100% beneficial owner of the subject property. His business
acumen is displayed in his founding and subsequent growth and sale of the renowned brewing company. In
addition, Mr. Phillips has invested in a variety of local real estate projects and currently holds a portfolio of
commercial real estate assets. Mr. Phillips, through consultation with Mr. Mat McLash, purchased the subject site
and has worked with Mat on the successful rezoning and planning of the subject project.
Owner Representation and Development Management
McLash Development (Mat McLash) has been engaged as the third-party development manager for the project.
With over 20 years of experience, McLash is currently managing several multi-family real estate development
projects in Greater Victoria, with a combined budget exceeding $100MM. Their responsibilities encompass all
aspects of the development process, including due diligence, acquisition analysis, proforma creation, planning,
rezoning, public consultation, permitting, RFP management, and consultant selection, as well as construction
oversight and client reporting.
Mr. McLash has successfully managed the acquisition, development, and operation, of a diverse range of
residential and mixed-use projects; from his many years as Vice President of Real Estate for a multinational
development company (Triple Five) to his more recent development work in Vancouver (OpenForm Properties),
which included the award-winning E15 project, which received the 2024 UDI Vancouver Award of Excellence for
ground-oriented housing. Mat has lived in Victoria for most of the last 7 years and he is fortunate to enjoy
numerous deep, long-standing relationships in Greater Victoria’s real estate community. Mr. McLash has strong
connections with key industry stakeholders, as he is also focused on acquiring prime property locations on
Vancouver Island for the future development of high-quality multifamily rental assets over the long term.
Mat McLash has been an important stakeholder since project inception, contributing his extensive expertise in all
phases of real estate development, from acquisitions to operations, and playing a key role in driving the project
forward. Mat has joined the project on behalf of the beneficial owner, Matt Phillips. The two have shared a
professional relationship since 2015, when Mat relocated to Victoria and worked out of the same office building
as Matt Phillips.

Construction Financing, Crestview Residences 4
Construction
Farmer Construction, headquartered in Victoria, BC, has been engaged as the contractor for the project under a
CCDC 5B construction management contract. With over 70 years of experience, the firm specializes in delivering

project.
Guarantee
A personal guarantee will provided by Mr. Matt Phillips (100% beneficial owner - $112MM PNW), along with a

− The active development manager has a strong and clear track record of delivering projects of similar and

Weaknesses

company to assist lease-up.

Greater Victoria
Located on the southern extremity of Vancouver Island, the Capital Region of Greater Victoria comprises a total
area of nearly 2,400 square kilometres and is comprised of 13 incorporated municipalities and 3 unincorporated
electoral areas. The region stretches from Saturna Island on the east, takes in Greater Victoria and the Saanich
Peninsula, and includes that part of Vancouver Island lying south of the Malahat Mountain range and east of Port
Renfrew. The City of Victoria is geographically small at the southernmost tip of the Capital Region and has the
highest density of all 13 municipalities.
Overall, Victoria has historically been considered a desirable location in terms of natural features and overall
lifestyle with a high proportion of retirees; however, wages and well-paid job opportunities have been limited

Construction Financing, Crestview Residences 13
especially for the younger demographic compared to larger cities such as Vancouver and Toronto. The increased
ability to work remotely has allowed many individuals to reside in Victoria while maintaining their remote work
positions abroad. This had led to an influx of potential purchasers, which paired with historically low interest
rates from 2020 to early 2022 resulted in substantial housing price increases; however, pricing has stabilized
since, likely due to interest rate increases that have increased mortgage costs, reducing buyers purchasing
power.
Town of Esquimalt
The Town of Esquimalt occupies the central portion of a large peninsula, west of the City of Victoria, on the south
end of Vancouver Island. Incorporated in 1912, it has an area of 7.08 square kilometres and a population of
17,533 (Based on 2021 Census Statistics). Esquimalt shares the peninsula with Victoria West, a mostly residential
suburb of the City of Victoria, on the east, and View Royal, a small mainly residential area. It is bound by the
Gorge Waterway to the north and by Victoria and Esquimalt Harbour to the south.
The majority of residential development in Esquimalt is characterized by single family homes and medium
density multi-family apartment buildings. It has historically been known as a lower income neighbourhood with
older stock, apart from the area surrounding the various waterways. In recent years, Esquimalt has increasingly
become home to mid end single family homes and mid end apartment buildings. This is in part due to being
more affordable compared to the neighbouring City of Victoria. Overall, the neighbourhood is in a transitional
stage from lower income to a more desirable area for commercial and residential use, with an improving rental
stock and good proximity to most amenities. New development along the waterfront has improved Esquimalt
and surrounding areas; however, the Esquimalt core and non-waterfront areas are still associated with older
inventory and low to middle income residents. Gentrification is likely the next phase in this area's evolution.
Subject Property (pinned) within Old Esquimalt
The Subject Property is well located in a commercial hub of the Old Esquimalt neighbourhood. The area consists
of predominately multifamily and commercial development along Esquimalt Road given its higher trafficked
location. However, older single family single family and attached housing found nearby to the north and south.
Due to the Subject’s central location, it is within walking distance to nearby commercial and public amenities as
well as public transportation routes. There are redevelopment projects underway near the Subject along

Downtown Victoria, the Esquimalt, Gorge, and Burnside neighbourhoods are becoming increasingly seen as a
viable alternative for both residential and commercial purposes.
Competing Developments
Esquimalt has experienced a significant surge in multifamily housing construction, particularly along the
Esquimalt Road corridor. Once completed, the subject property will contribute to the approximately 900 new
homes anticipated for delivery between 2025 and 2027. This growth is driven by eight projects directly fronting
Esquimalt Road. These projects are adding substantial density to a key thoroughfare that connects Victoria’s Vic
West neighbourhood to CFB Esquimalt, while also serving as the primary commercial hub of the Township of
Esquimalt. Growth in rental housing in Esquimalt is needed, as referenced by the 1.5% vacancy rate (CMHC)
compared to the whole of Victoria at 2.6%. The injection of supply should raise the vacancy rate in Esquimalt
from the lowest zone in Metro Victoria to a healthier position in line with the area’s average. An illustrative map

Housing Market, CMHC
Highlights from CMHC’s Fall 2024 Rental Market Report (Victoria)
The overall vacancy rate reached its highest level since 2013 while vacancies remained low in the city
centre.
The overall vacancy rate increased to 2.6% with significant increases in Langford/View Royal/Colwood (Zone 7)
while remaining low in the City of Victoria (Table 1.1.1). In Langford, a 24.8% increase in the purpose-built rental
universe pushed vacancy rates up. New units outside of the city centre tend to have longer lease-up times, which
likely drove the increase.
Supported by a substantial government sector, the labour market remains resilient with low unemployment
unlike nearby major markets like Vancouver, Calgary and Edmonton. This bolstered rental demand in Victoria.
Students drive rental demand in the Saanich and Oak Bay areas near the University of Victoria. Vacancy rates in
both zones were well below the CMA average as rental supply has not kept up with demand historically. The
number of units under construction in Saanich roughly doubled from 2023 to 2024, signaling more rental supply
growth in the next 12 to 24 months.
High demand pushed rent growth, worsening affordability
An influx of new rental units contributed to increases in average rents especially in Langford. Rents for 2-
bedroom units in Victoria surpassed those of Toronto, making Victoria the second most expensive market in
Canada, behind Vancouver
Same-sample average 2-bedroom rent growth declined to 3.6% in 2024 (Table 1.1.5). A substantial increase in
supply and the higher vacancy rates contributed to slower rent growth despite strong demand.
Turnover remained above the CMA average in the Langford and Sidney areas. Renters living in these areas are
likely to be renting at a rate closer to market rents and have fewer incentives to stay in place. Meanwhile,
turnover rates declined in the City of Victoria, reflecting tighter market conditions.
Purpose-built rental growth accelerated especially in Langford
The purpose-built rental universe expanded by 5.7% in 2024 (Table 1.1.3), above the recent historical pace. Units
added in the area stretching from Langford to Sooke accounted for over half of the increase, while units added in
the city accounted for less than one third.

1.2 Objective
This Stage 2 PSI was conducted to determine the presence or absence of PCOCs related to the
two above APECs.
1.3 Scope of Work
The scope of work for this Stage 2 PSI was limited to the following;
 Reviewing available previous environmental reports for the Site, including the previous
Stage 1 PSI, verifying the overall findings and determining whether environmental
conditions have altered since the historical investigation(s);
 Developing a Health and Safety Plan;
 Completing a BC One Call and overseeing a Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) scan within
the vicinity of the APECs to ensure safe clearance of underground utilities, identify
obstructions for sampling locations;
 Conducting a UST investigation, with advancement of one on-Site borehole within the
former nest;
 Advancing a borehole to install a groundwater monitoring well and soil vapour probe to
characterize environmental media on Site;
 Collecting representative soil, groundwater and soil vapour samples from the boreholes,
well and vapour probe, at discrete and variable depths;
 Submitting selected samples to an accredited laboratory for analysis of PCOCs;
 Reviewing the analytical results from the subsurface investigation, with comparison to
current applicable BC CSR standards; and
 Interpreting, reporting and recommending on the above findings.
This Stage 2 PSI was conducted in general accordance with the BC Ministry of Environment and
Climate Change Strategy (ENV) Environmental Management Act (EMA) and the Contaminated
Sites Regulation (CSR). Additionally, this report has been prepared in general accordance with
the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) Environmental Site Assessment (ESA)
guidelines and the Canadian Standards Association (CSA) Standard Z769-00 Phase II ESA
guidelines.
