3.0 Scope of Services
BTY’s approach to providing successful Project Monitoring Services during project delivery is based upon our
extensive experience of providing these services to a number of financial institutions across Canada.
Please note that the following scope of work is based on BTY’s experience in the Project Monitoring role. This
scope is not definitive; the final scope of work will be agreed upon with the Lender in accordance with their terms
of engagement. In the absence of a terms of engagement, the scope of service will be in accordance with the
requirements set out in the financing agreement between the Developer and the Lender.
Budget Review
• Review and summarize the Lender’s Commitment Letter and QS Engagement Letter to confirm the
requirements outlined by the Lender and conditions precedent to the loan agreement, that relate to our
scope of services.
• Undertake a review of the construction costs and development costs of the project, based on the
drawings, specifications and project budget submitted by the Developer, to ensure that all relevant hard
and soft costs have been included in the Project Budget. (Note that we will not carry out a full
comparative cost estimate, unless specifically requested to do so, which would be in addition to our
proposed fee).
• Review the quotations and fixed price contracts received, or if not finalized, review the sub-trade tenders
for each section of the works, to assess the impact on the construction budget.
• Review the soft cost elements of work and comment on their reasonableness, including a review of the
substantiating information provided for the consultants, municipal costs, marketing allowances,
development costs and contingency.
• Assess the validity of the construction schedule duration and cash flow, as provided by the Developer.
We will also prepare a detailed cash flow to assess the estimated draw amounts from the loan, which
will be updated with each Progress Claim report.
• Undertake a review of the geotechnical and environment reports, to ensure that the recommendations
outlined in these reports have been incorporated in the project design.

or whether funded through a separate loan facility.
• Provide a summary and brief description of the key members of the Design Team.
• If required by the Lender, undertake a review of the sale agreements, to confirm that details of the
contracts and deposits received reflect the details identified on the sales summary. (Note that this is not
for legal purposes and would be in addition to our proposed fee).
Progress Claims
We will undertake a periodic review of the Developer’s request for funds, typically on a monthly basis, to determine
reasonableness in the application for payment and confirm that the remaining budget is adequate to complete the
project. This will include the following:
• Undertake a review of the Developer’s claim in comparison to the works completed on site to ensure
that the percentage claimed is reasonable. This will include a review of the major invoices when made
available.
• Review all cash allowances and approved change orders when provided by the Developer and confirm
their impact on the project budget.
• Outline any further adjustments which may be required to the project budget or the claim request to
ensure that the cost-to-complete is reasonable.
• Incorporate a copy of the Developer’s and Contractor’s statutory declarations, and Lender forms as
necessary, which confirm that the holdback is in place, the funds received to date have been used for
the project and that all bills have been paid.
• Undertake a review of cancelled cheques and bank statements, if requested by the Lender, to ensure
that the required equity amount has been paid into the project. Review cancelled cheques and accounts
payable listings periodically, if requested by the Lender, to ensure all accounts are up to date. This review
may be for costs over an agreed threshold with the Lender.
• Incorporate a copy of the Project Consultant’s Certificate, signed by the Architect as lead consultant, to
confirm that the works have been carried out in accordance with the drawings and specifications. BTY
Group is not qualified to provide confirmation that the works are being constructed in accordance with
the approved drawings.
• Carry out an inspection of the works completed on site and provide a summary of the status of works
within our progress claim report. Review this against the monthly claim to ensure that the percentage
being claimed is reasonable.
• Provide a summary of any materials being claimed off-site or deposits to be paid. Review the
corresponding invoice and cancelled cheque following payment.

TREE PRESERVATION MEASURES
1. Site meeting to review Tree Plan: Before demolition and site preparation begin, the owner and contractor shall meet with the arborist to review the placement of fencing
and other tree protection measures within this plan.
a) The Project Arborist shall clearly mark the boundaries of all areas to be fenced and protected.
b) Access routes and areas for trade parking and materials storage will be identified with the contractor.
2. Tree Fencing:
a) Tree protection fencing shall be installed to the City of Esquimalt standards at the locations indicated on this drawing prior to demolition or building permit being issued
(see fencing detail on plan).
b) Tree protection fencing and armouring shall be maintained in good condition throughout the duration of the project.
c) Requests to temporarily remove or move tree fencing must be reviewed by the project arborist for approval.
3. Soil armouring: If it is not possible to fence the entire PRZ, the unprotected portion of the PRZ shall be armoured with 3/4" plywood or a temporary cover of geo-textile and
200mm of road-base, moderately compacted with a plate compactor. (See drawing for recommended soil armouring locations.)
4. Arborist supervision: The project arborist shall be on site during demolition to supervise work in sensitive areas as indicated on the Tree Plan in lieu of erecting tree
barrier fencing.
5. Root & branch pruning and protection:
a) Any tree roots or branches damaged during site work shall be pruned back to undamaged tissue by the arborist.
b) The vertical face of excavated cuts adjacent to the TPAs shall be securely covered with non-permeable fabric by the project arborist to prevent soil desiccation and
erosion.
6. Temporary access: If temporary access is required within a tree protection area (TPA), the contractor shall notify the project arborist in advance and review the access
requirements and any additional protective measures prescribed by the arborist.

Construction Financing, Crestview Residences 2
Executive Summary
Loan Request
Request for first mortgage high-leverage construction financing in the amount of $23,130,000 (85% LTC) to
support the development of a 59-unit apartment project in Esquimalt, BC. Municipal council awarded 3
rd 
reading
to the subject property on November 4, 2024, with the Development Permit application submitted thereafter.
The project is expected to break ground in June of this year and the sponsor is currently going through a detailed
tender of costs and building permit submission.
Purpose
This construction financing will be refinanced upon project completion with CMHC-insured financing through the
MLI Select program or the sale of the asset. This approach enables the Borrower flexibility to finance / sell based
on rental rates at the time of completion. i.e. the sponsor would be able to secure CMHC financing at the market
rate at the time of project delivery instead of anchoring to lower rental rates today.
Current financing on the two lots is $2,100,000 with a 1-year term at a floating rate. The request is to provide a
construction loan with a land advance to replace the existing loans, and commence construction, with the 59-unit
project expected to be completed in 24-months from funding.
Subject Lands and Project
The subject lands consist of 16,627 sf (0.38 acres), with frontage along Esquimalt Road and are currently
improved with two residential structures, which are slated for demolition prior to the first construction advance.
The site received third reading approval for rezoning to CD No. 158 (Comprehensive Development) with no
objections.
Upon completion, Crestview - the subject property, will comprise a 59-unit, six-story wood-framed apartment
building atop two levels of underground parking. The first parking level will be partially at grade with the first
floor, resulting in a partial main floor. This level will house the main lobby/entrance, as well as an amenity/social
room equipped with a kitchen and washroom. The units will range in size from 418 to 923 sf, with an average size
of 568 sf. All suites will feature air conditioning and modern finishes. At grade, the subject will include outdoor
amenity space including green space, an outdoor patio dining / common area with barbeques. The building
offers a net rentable area of 33,500 sf and a gross buildable area of 43,235 sf.
Loan Advance Particulars
No land lift is being injected into the capital stack. We recommend and are open to considering a land advance to
assure title is secured by the construction lender.
Key metrics supporting the request are:
- Debt yield of 5.74% on the proposed loan
- Loan exposure per door of $392K.
- PSF (NLA) loan exposure of $690, and $535 PBSF.
- 85% LTC and 77% LTV as-complete.

Construction Financing, Crestview Residences 3
The construction loan provides palatable loan exposure on a relatively straightforward wood frame build. The
borrower acquired the site in 2020 for $2,800,000 and has subsequently commenced the rezoning process to
accommodate the project. The land is being contributed to the project at cost, excluding carrying costs to date.
Exit Strategy
At project completion, the Borrower will takeout the conventional financing with a CMHC insured loan through
the MLI Select program or sell the asset. Depending on the Borrower’s preference to either commit affordable
units for higher leverage financing or rent at market rates with lower gross loan dollars, a viable takeout option is
achievable in both scenarios, with no rental growth projections. We have supplied CMHC underwriting which
has been conservatively applied on the exit using a base case 40-year amortization period and 4% interest rate
with the spread between the proposed construction loan and potential takeout loan being a minimum of
$1.3MM +/-.
Sponsorship
Owner
Matt Phillips, founder of Phillips Brewing, is the 100% beneficial owner of the subject property. His business
acumen is displayed in his founding and subsequent growth and sale of the renowned brewing company. In
addition, Mr. Phillips has invested in a variety of local real estate projects and currently holds a portfolio of
commercial real estate assets. Mr. Phillips, through consultation with Mr. Mat McLash, purchased the subject site
and has worked with Mat on the successful rezoning and planning of the subject project.
Owner Representation and Development Management
McLash Development (Mat McLash) has been engaged as the third-party development manager for the project.
With over 20 years of experience, McLash is currently managing several multi-family real estate development
projects in Greater Victoria, with a combined budget exceeding $100MM. Their responsibilities encompass all
aspects of the development process, including due diligence, acquisition analysis, proforma creation, planning,
rezoning, public consultation, permitting, RFP management, and consultant selection, as well as construction
oversight and client reporting.
Mr. McLash has successfully managed the acquisition, development, and operation, of a diverse range of
residential and mixed-use projects; from his many years as Vice President of Real Estate for a multinational
development company (Triple Five) to his more recent development work in Vancouver (OpenForm Properties),
which included the award-winning E15 project, which received the 2024 UDI Vancouver Award of Excellence for
ground-oriented housing. Mat has lived in Victoria for most of the last 7 years and he is fortunate to enjoy
numerous deep, long-standing relationships in Greater Victoria’s real estate community. Mr. McLash has strong
connections with key industry stakeholders, as he is also focused on acquiring prime property locations on
Vancouver Island for the future development of high-quality multifamily rental assets over the long term.
Mat McLash has been an important stakeholder since project inception, contributing his extensive expertise in all
phases of real estate development, from acquisitions to operations, and playing a key role in driving the project
forward. Mat has joined the project on behalf of the beneficial owner, Matt Phillips. The two have shared a
professional relationship since 2015, when Mat relocated to Victoria and worked out of the same office building
as Matt Phillips.

Construction Financing, Crestview Residences 4
Construction
Farmer Construction, headquartered in Victoria, BC, has been engaged as the contractor for the project under a
CCDC 5B construction management contract. With over 70 years of experience, the firm specializes in delivering
comprehensive construction management services, including pre-construction planning, budgeting, scheduling,
and on-site supervision. Their role ensures effective coordination and oversight throughout all phases of the
project.
Guarantee
A personal guarantee will provided by Mr. Matt Phillips (100% beneficial owner - $112MM PNW), along with a
corporate guarantee from his holding company, 0913625 B.C. Ltd. Mr. Phillips holds 80% of his PNW in highly
liquid public and private equities, with the remainder contributed from a real estate portfolio of income
producing assets, as well as business interests.
Mr. Phillips is the founder of Phillips Brewing, a craft brewery established in Victoria in 2001. Under his
leadership, the company has grown significantly, expanding its reach across North America and operating out of
a headquarters spanning an entire block in Victoria's Old Town. In addition to his extensive business experience,
Mr. Phillips possesses local real estate acumen and currently holds four income producing commercial assets
comprising 84k sf. This is the first development project of this scale for Mr. Phillips, hence engaging Mr. McLash
to lead the development process.
Summary & Recommendations
Strengths
− The active development manager has a strong and clear track record of delivering projects of similar and
greater scale in the Victoria market.
− Strong guarantor covenant, with highly liquid assets alone nearing 400% of the loan request.
− Very strong contractor in Farmer Construction
− No land lift as a part of the capital stack.
Weaknesses
− High leverage request.
− First ground up build for Mr. Phillips.
− Potential increased rental universe and slower absorption.
Mitigants
− Contractor has reviewed budget projections and has extensive track record in Victoria.
− Conservative rental projections to necessitate takeout financing and established property management
company to assist lease-up.
− Low local vacancy rate and attractive location provide strong fundamentals for demand. Vacancy
allowance has been conservatively inputted above market and the project still provides strong returns.

Location Overview
Location
The subject property is located along the Esquimalt corridor in a commercial hub approximately 4 minutes from
downtown Victoria. The site is very well serviced by transit, and the Songhees walkway to downtown Victoria is
just steps away. Nearby walkable amenities include Place Valentine shopping centre, Shoppers drugmart, the
Cask and Keg liquor store and Westbay Marine Village.
Subject site (pinned) in relation to Downtown Victoria.

Public Transit
The subject property is well-served by public transit, located just steps from bus stop #100283, which services
the 800 block of Esquimalt Road. Route 15, with service approximately every 15 minutes M-F, provides a direct
connection to the University of Victoria via major arterial roads in Victoria. Along its route, the bus passes key
amenities, including various schools, the Royal Jubilee Hospital, and Camosun College - the region’s second-
largest post-secondary institution.
This high level of connectivity makes the property an attractive option for a diverse range of tenants, including
downtown Victoria workers, hospital staff, UVic and Camosun students, and families with school-aged children
who can utilize public transit for their commute. A transit map for Route 15 is provided below:
Subject site (starred)
Greater Victoria
Located on the southern extremity of Vancouver Island, the Capital Region of Greater Victoria comprises a total
area of nearly 2,400 square kilometres and is comprised of 13 incorporated municipalities and 3 unincorporated
electoral areas. The region stretches from Saturna Island on the east, takes in Greater Victoria and the Saanich
Peninsula, and includes that part of Vancouver Island lying south of the Malahat Mountain range and east of Port
Renfrew. The City of Victoria is geographically small at the southernmost tip of the Capital Region and has the
highest density of all 13 municipalities.
Overall, Victoria has historically been considered a desirable location in terms of natural features and overall
lifestyle with a high proportion of retirees; however, wages and well-paid job opportunities have been limited

Construction Financing, Crestview Residences 13
especially for the younger demographic compared to larger cities such as Vancouver and Toronto. The increased
ability to work remotely has allowed many individuals to reside in Victoria while maintaining their remote work
positions abroad. This had led to an influx of potential purchasers, which paired with historically low interest
rates from 2020 to early 2022 resulted in substantial housing price increases; however, pricing has stabilized
since, likely due to interest rate increases that have increased mortgage costs, reducing buyers purchasing
power.
Town of Esquimalt
The Town of Esquimalt occupies the central portion of a large peninsula, west of the City of Victoria, on the south
end of Vancouver Island. Incorporated in 1912, it has an area of 7.08 square kilometres and a population of
17,533 (Based on 2021 Census Statistics). Esquimalt shares the peninsula with Victoria West, a mostly residential
suburb of the City of Victoria, on the east, and View Royal, a small mainly residential area. It is bound by the
Gorge Waterway to the north and by Victoria and Esquimalt Harbour to the south.
The majority of residential development in Esquimalt is characterized by single family homes and medium
density multi-family apartment buildings. It has historically been known as a lower income neighbourhood with
older stock, apart from the area surrounding the various waterways. In recent years, Esquimalt has increasingly
become home to mid end single family homes and mid end apartment buildings. This is in part due to being
more affordable compared to the neighbouring City of Victoria. Overall, the neighbourhood is in a transitional
stage from lower income to a more desirable area for commercial and residential use, with an improving rental
stock and good proximity to most amenities. New development along the waterfront has improved Esquimalt
and surrounding areas; however, the Esquimalt core and non-waterfront areas are still associated with older
inventory and low to middle income residents. Gentrification is likely the next phase in this area's evolution.
Subject Property (pinned) within Old Esquimalt
The Subject Property is well located in a commercial hub of the Old Esquimalt neighbourhood. The area consists
of predominately multifamily and commercial development along Esquimalt Road given its higher trafficked
location. However, older single family single family and attached housing found nearby to the north and south.
Due to the Subject’s central location, it is within walking distance to nearby commercial and public amenities as
well as public transportation routes. There are redevelopment projects underway near the Subject along

Construction Financing, Crestview Residences 14
Esquimalt Road as well as higher density redevelopment planned in the near future. Due to higher rental rates in
Downtown Victoria, the Esquimalt, Gorge, and Burnside neighbourhoods are becoming increasingly seen as a
viable alternative for both residential and commercial purposes.
Competing Developments
Esquimalt has experienced a significant surge in multifamily housing construction, particularly along the
Esquimalt Road corridor. Once completed, the subject property will contribute to the approximately 900 new
homes anticipated for delivery between 2025 and 2027. This growth is driven by eight projects directly fronting
Esquimalt Road. These projects are adding substantial density to a key thoroughfare that connects Victoria’s Vic
West neighbourhood to CFB Esquimalt, while also serving as the primary commercial hub of the Township of
Esquimalt. Growth in rental housing in Esquimalt is needed, as referenced by the 1.5% vacancy rate (CMHC)
compared to the whole of Victoria at 2.6%. The injection of supply should raise the vacancy rate in Esquimalt
from the lowest zone in Metro Victoria to a healthier position in line with the area’s average. An illustrative map
of upcoming developments is available below:
This new housing and rental supply aligns with the township’s commitment to economic development through
the 2023-2025 Economic Development Action Plan. This plan aims to attract businesses, create jobs, stimulate
investment, and enhance the overall quality of life for residents, supporting Esquimalt's vision of becoming a
vibrant, unique, and inclusive community.
Looking ahead to project lease-up, it is reasonable to anticipate increased demand driven by a natural flow of
investment into the subject neighbourhood. However, the substantial incoming supply has tempered rental
growth assumptions. Partnering with a top-tier property management group will be a priority, ensuring effective

marketing during and prior to project completion. The relatively small number of units in the subject property
renting at conservative rates should mitigate vacancy risks, supporting the NOI at the time of takeout with term

4.4 Groundwater Investigation
The sections below outline the methodology used for the groundwater investigation.
4.4.1 Monitoring Well Installation
BH19-2 was completed as groundwater monitoring well. The location of the well was based on
the proximity of APEC2 identified in the Stage 1 PSI and can be referenced in Figure 4.
The well was constructed with washed and wrapped 50 mm (2") diameter, schedule 80, flush-
threaded PVC. Slotted screen casings were installed at the bottom of the hole, with a maximum
length of 1.5 metres (5’). Solid PVC blank casings were used for the remaining upper portion of
the hole. The base of the monitoring well was plugged with a PVC, threaded cap. The space
surrounding each screened length was backfilled with clean silica filter sand, from the base of the
well to 0.3 metres (1') above the screened section. A minimum of 0.5 metres of hydrated bentonite
chips was added, creating a bentonite seal to prevent infiltration from the surface. The monitoring
well was capped with a 50 mm (2") J-plug and covered with a cemented, steel, flush-mounted
road box. The wells was installed in the borehole at 3.1 m bgs. Well completion details are
included on the borehole logs, which can be referenced in Appendix B.
4.4.2 Monitoring Well Development
The well was developed to remove drilling debris and fine solids from the well screen and filter
zone surrounding the screen. If a well is not developed, the drilling debris and fine particles may
influence the water level response time, hydraulic conductivity estimates, and groundwater quality
samples. A standard-capacity Waterra inertial pumping system activated by a Waterra Hydrolift
was used for well development. A 1.6 cm outer diameter HDPE Waterra tubing was fitted with a
surge block and foot valve. Starting at the bottom of the screen, the foot valve/surge block was
placed at successively shallower locations until the top of the screen was reached so that the
entire screened zone was developed. Development at each interval continued until diminishing
sediment returns had been reached and the extracted water was relatively clear. The surge block
was then removed, the foot valve was placed at the top of the screen, and pumping was resumed.
Water volume, sediment quantity, pH, and electrical conductivity were recorded. Lastly, the foot

5.0 QUALITY ASSURANCE / QUALITY CONTROL
5.1 Field QA/QC
WES Ltd. employs an established field protocol, including approved techniques for sampling,
sample storage, shipping, handling and the collection of field duplicates. The QA/QC field program
includes documentation protocols for sample collection, transport and sample storage; field
protocols to ensure no risk of cross-contamination of samples throughout the sampling events;
and logging of all routine and anomalous occurrences that may introduce bias.
To minimize the potential for cross-contamination between samples and ensure reliable results,
the following QA/QC procedures were utilized by WES:
Soil
 Soil samples were collected by hand or with a cleaned trowel directly off the auger, from
distinct soil zones, at representative borehole depths.
 Using nitrile gloves, soil samples were transferred and thumb-packed into laboratory
cleaned 125 ml glass soil sample jars, secured with a teflon lid.
 Soil samples selected for analysis of VOC, BTEX and/or VPH analysis were collected
using Terra Core 5g samplers into duplicate 40 ml glass vials, with methanol preservative.
Groundwater
 Groundwater samples selected for L/HEPH analysis were collected in duplicate 60 mL
amber vials, with sodium bisulphate preservative.

 Groundwater samples selected for PAH analysis were collected in 500 ml amber glass
bottles.
 Groundwater samples selected for VOC, BTEX and/or VPH analysis were collected in
triplicate 40 ml, clear glass vials, with sodium bisulphate preservative.
 The water samples analyzed for dissolved metals were collected in 250 ml plastic bottles.
Each soil and groundwater sample was appropriately logged and labelled, then placed in an
artificially cooled and insulated container (soils and groundwater) or a sealed container (soil
vapours), with a signed chain of custody form, prior to shipment to the laboratory for analysis. All
parameters were analyzed within the applicable laboratory holding times.

Laboratory analysis for soil and groundwater was completed by CARO Analytical, Richmond,
British Columbia. The laboratory employs methods approved by the Ministry of Environment and

agencies, including the Canadian Association for Laboratory Accreditation (CALA) and the
Standards Council of Canada (SCC). To ensure data is of the highest quality, CARO include
analysis of duplicates, blanks and reference materials in each sample batch.
The results of the laboratory QA/QC analyses and a copy of the analytical data reports is
presented in Appendix C.
6.0 RESULTS
6.1 Field Observations
The geological conditions of the subsurface were observed and logged during drilling. Non-native,
odourous fill sands were encountered overlying silty clays within the former UST nest. BH19-2
and BH19-3 were characterized by a layer of topsoil overlying permeable course sand with trace
silts, and at depth silty clays. Bedrock was inferred at these locations at 2.4 to 3.0 m. Borehole
logs are available in Appendix B.
Groundwater was not encountered during drilling; however, the groundwater table was measured
between 1.60 and 1.93 m bgs upon stabilization of the well.
Total Volatile Organic Compound (tVOC) head-space readings were taken for the soil samples
prior to selection for submission of analyses to the laboratory. The handheld MiniRae 3000 Photo
Ionization Detector (PID), measured from 6.5 to 15.7 ppm tVOC across all soil samples collected.

7.0 DISCUSSION
Soil samples from the tank nest (19-1), and groundwater from the on-Site well (19-2) were
collected as part of this Stage 2 PSI to investigate the presence or absence of PCOCs related to
the two APECs identified in the Stage 1 PSI. A summary of the findings for each APEC is
presented below.
APEC1 – Former Residential Heating Oil UST
Field observations from the drilling program demonstrated olfactory presence of hydrocarbons
within the fill sands of the former UST nest. The soil samples were pre-screened in the field, and

Stage 2 Preliminary Site Investigation Project Number: 18075
861 & 863-865 Esquimalt Road, Esquimalt, BC 14 Date: March 26, 2019
the sample (BH19-1-4) with the highest tVOC’s was selected for analysis. PCOC concentrations
in the analyzed soil sample demonstrated detectable EPH and PAH’s, however each parameter
was within the applicable CSR RL 
HDR 
standard. Should redevelopment at the Site occur, this soil
may not be suitable for relocation due to visual and olfactory concerns.
APEC2 – Off-Site Schedule 2 Activities – Auto Repair and Servicing Station
Analysis of groundwater from the well at 19-2, placed within the northeastern corner of the Site,
nearest to the off-Site APEC, initially demonstrated detectable levels of EPH’s and PAH’s,
including on exceedance of the parameter LEPHw (3,530 μ/L) for protection of Aquatic Marine
Life (500 μg/L). Sample MW1-0219 was repeated at the laboratory, returning similar results.
However, after groundwater purging and sampling was repeated on March 11 
th 
, 2019, non-
detectable results of LEPHw and PAHs were returned. In order to confirm the first groundwater
sample was false, a third purging and sampling event was completed March 20 
th 
, 2019 with
repeated non-detectable results. Based on the data from the two follow up sampling events,
groundwater is not considered an issue at location 19-2.
The soil vapour probe installed at 19-3 was found to contain vacuum conditions due to an elevated
groundwater table, and therefore was not available for testing within the timeframe of this report.
The analytical results, in conjunction with the field observations indicate that there are no on-Site
concerns for PCOCs related to off-Site APEC2.

The following section displays the quality control (QC) data that is associated with your sample data. Groups of samples are prepared
in ìbatchesî and analyzed in conjunction with QC samples that ensure your data is of the highest quality. Common QC types include:
ï Method Blank (Blk): A blank sample that undergoes sample processing identical to that carried out for the test samples. Method
blank results are used to assess contamination from the laboratory environment and reagents.
ï Duplicate (Dup): An additional or second portion of a randomly selected sample in the analytical run carried through the entire
analytical process. Duplicates provide a measure of the analytical method's precision (reproducibility).
ï Blank Spike (BS): A sample of known concentration which undergoes processing identical to that carried out for test samples, a l s o
referred to as a laboratory control sample (LCS). Blank spikes provide a measure of the analytical method's accuracy.
ï Matrix Spike (MS): A second aliquot of sample is fortified with with a known concentration of target analytes and carried through
the entire analytical process. Matrix spikes evaluate potential matrix effects that may affect the analyte recovery.
ï Reference Material (SRM): A homogenous material of similar matrix to the samples, certified for the parameter(s) listed.
Reference Materials ensure that the analytical process is adequate to achieve acceptable recoveries of the parameter(s) tested.
Each QC type is analyzed at a 5-10% frequency, i.e. one blank/duplicate/spike for every 10-20 samples. For all types of QC, the
specified recovery (% Rec) and relative percent difference (RPD) limits are derived from long-term method performance averages
and/or prescribed by the reference method.

The following section displays the quality control (QC) data that is associated with your sample data. Groups of samples are prepared
in “batches” and analyzed in conjunction with QC samples that ensure your data is of the highest quality. Common QC types include:
• Method Blank (Blk): A blank sample that undergoes sample processing identical to that carried out for the test samples. Method
blank results are used to assess contamination from the laboratory environment and reagents.
• Duplicate (Dup): An additional or second portion of a randomly selected sample in the analytical run carried through the entire
analytical process. Duplicates provide a measure of the analytical method's precision (reproducibility).
• Blank Spike (BS): A sample of known concentration which undergoes processing identical to that carried out for test samples, a l s o
referred to as a laboratory control sample (LCS). Blank spikes provide a measure of the analytical method's accuracy.
• Matrix Spike (MS): A second aliquot of sample is fortified with with a known concentration of target analytes and carried through
the entire analytical process. Matrix spikes evaluate potential matrix effects that may affect the analyte recovery.
• Reference Material (SRM): A homogenous material of similar matrix to the samples, certified for the parameter(s) listed.
Reference Materials ensure that the analytical process is adequate to achieve acceptable recoveries of the parameter(s) tested.
Each QC type is analyzed at a 5-10% frequency, i.e. one blank/duplicate/spike for every 10-20 samples. For all types of QC, the
specified recovery (% Rec) and relative percent difference (RPD) limits are derived from long-term method performance averages
and/or prescribed by the reference method.

The following section displays the quality control (QC) data that is associated with your sample data. Groups of samples are prepared
in ìbatchesî and analyzed in conjunction with QC samples that ensure your data is of the highest quality. Common QC types include:
ï Method Blank (Blk): A blank sample that undergoes sample processing identical to that carried out for the test samples. Method
blank results are used to assess contamination from the laboratory environment and reagents.
ï Duplicate (Dup): An additional or second portion of a randomly selected sample in the analytical run carried through the entire
analytical process. Duplicates provide a measure of the analytical method's precision (reproducibility).
ï Blank Spike (BS): A sample of known concentration which undergoes processing identical to that carried out for test samples, a l s o
referred to as a laboratory control sample (LCS). Blank spikes provide a measure of the analytical method's accuracy.
ï Matrix Spike (MS): A second aliquot of sample is fortified with with a known concentration of target analytes and carried through
the entire analytical process. Matrix spikes evaluate potential matrix effects that may affect the analyte recovery.
ï Reference Material (SRM): A homogenous material of similar matrix to the samples, certified for the parameter(s) listed.
Reference Materials ensure that the analytical process is adequate to achieve acceptable recoveries of the parameter(s) tested.
Each QC type is analyzed at a 5-10% frequency, i.e. one blank/duplicate/spike for every 10-20 samples. For all types of QC, the
specified recovery (% Rec) and relative percent difference (RPD) limits are derived from long-term method performance averages
and/or prescribed by the reference method.

The following section displays the quality control (QC) data that is associated with your sample data. Groups of samples are prepared
in ìbatchesî and analyzed in conjunction with QC samples that ensure your data is of the highest quality. Common QC types include:
ï Method Blank (Blk): A blank sample that undergoes sample processing identical to that carried out for the test samples. Method
blank results are used to assess contamination from the laboratory environment and reagents.
ï Duplicate (Dup): An additional or second portion of a randomly selected sample in the analytical run carried through the entire
analytical process. Duplicates provide a measure of the analytical method's precision (reproducibility).
ï Blank Spike (BS): A sample of known concentration which undergoes processing identical to that carried out for test samples, a l s o
referred to as a laboratory control sample (LCS). Blank spikes provide a measure of the analytical method's accuracy.
ï Matrix Spike (MS): A second aliquot of sample is fortified with with a known concentration of target analytes and carried through
the entire analytical process. Matrix spikes evaluate potential matrix effects that may affect the analyte recovery.
ï Reference Material (SRM): A homogenous material of similar matrix to the samples, certified for the parameter(s) listed.
Reference Materials ensure that the analytical process is adequate to achieve acceptable recoveries of the parameter(s) tested.
Each QC type is analyzed at a 5-10% frequency, i.e. one blank/duplicate/spike for every 10-20 samples. For all types of QC, the
specified recovery (% Rec) and relative percent difference (RPD) limits are derived from long-term method performance averages
and/or prescribed by the reference method.

The following section displays the quality control (QC) data that is associated with your sample data. Groups of samples are prepared
in ìbatchesî and analyzed in conjunction with QC samples that ensure your data is of the highest quality. Common QC types include:
ï Method Blank (Blk): A blank sample that undergoes sample processing identical to that carried out for the test samples. Method
blank results are used to assess contamination from the laboratory environment and reagents.
ï Duplicate (Dup): An additional or second portion of a randomly selected sample in the analytical run carried through the entire
analytical process. Duplicates provide a measure of the analytical method's precision (reproducibility).
ï Blank Spike (BS): A sample of known concentration which undergoes processing identical to that carried out for test samples, a l s o
referred to as a laboratory control sample (LCS). Blank spikes provide a measure of the analytical method's accuracy.
ï Matrix Spike (MS): A second aliquot of sample is fortified with with a known concentration of target analytes and carried through
the entire analytical process. Matrix spikes evaluate potential matrix effects that may affect the analyte recovery.
ï Reference Material (SRM): A homogenous material of similar matrix to the samples, certified for the parameter(s) listed.
Reference Materials ensure that the analytical process is adequate to achieve acceptable recoveries of the parameter(s) tested.
Each QC type is analyzed at a 5-10% frequency, i.e. one blank/duplicate/spike for every 10-20 samples. For all types of QC, the
specified recovery (% Rec) and relative percent difference (RPD) limits are derived from long-term method performance averages
and/or prescribed by the reference method.

DEFINITIONS
NOTE: All terms which are defined, and which are used throughout this document appear initalicized text beginning with a CAPITAL letter.
In this Contract the following definitions apply:
ADDITIONAL SERVICES
Those services which are not contemplated at the time of Contract execution and therefore cannot be identified then as being included in the
Contract but which, with the Client’s written permission, are added to the scope of services agreed to in the Contract.
CLIENT
The person or entity identified as such in the Contract.
CONSTRUCTION COST
For the purpose of percentage fee calculation, the Construction Cost is the contract price(s) of all project elements designed or specified by, or on
behalf of, or as a result of coordination of the Consultant, including cash allowances, building permit fees, changes, construction management
fees or other fees for the coordination and procurement of construction services, and all applicable taxes, e[cluding value-added taxes, whether
recoverable or not.
Where there is no contract price for all or part of the project, or if construction does not proceed, the Construction Cost shall be the statement of
the probable cost of construction, as agreed to in writing by the Client and the Consultant, at market prices at the anticipated time of construction.
Construction Cost excludes the following:
• the compensation of the Consultant and the Consultant’s Sub-Consultants,
• other professional fees which are the responsibility of the Client, or
• the land cost, land development charges or other costs which are the responsibility of the Client.
In the event that the Client furnishes labour or material below market costs, or recycled materials are used, for purposes of establishing the
Consultant’s fees the Construction Cost includes the cost of materials and labour necessary to complete the work as if materials had been new and as
if labour had been paid for at market prices at the anticipated time of construction.
CONSULTANT
The registered architect or professional engineer, licensed in British Columbia, engaged by the Client, to provide professional services in the
discipline(s) designated on the Contract form. The Consultant includes the Consultant's officers, directors, employees, representatives and Sub-
Consultants.
CONTRACT FOR CONSULTANT SERVICES (CONTRACT)

General Conditions, and attachments where applicable. Unless and to the extent superseded by a more detailed contract, this Contract governs
regarding the Consultant’s services and Client’s obligations.
INSTRUMENTS OF SERVICE
The documents prepared by or on behalf of the Consultant including but not limited to plans, designs, sketches, drawings, models, graphic
representations, reports, specifications and opinions.
MANAGING CONSULTANT

project. The Managing Consultant is (as applicable to the project) the “Coordinating Registered Professional” as defined under the building code or
bylaw and the “Consultant” as defined under Canadian Construction Documents Committee (CCDC) Standard Construction Contract Forms.
OTHER CONSULTANTS

PROJECT BUDGET
The Client’s estimated total expenditure for the entire project. It may include, but not be limited to, the Construction Cost, professional fees, costs of
land, and all other costs to the Client for the project.
REIMBURSABLE EXPENSES

Further to the Architects Act and Bylaws 28 and 29, the AIBC Council has endorsed an amended approach
with regard to both the recommended net architectural percentage fees and the scope of basic architectural
services in the “Market Multiple-Residential Sector”. This approach represents a professionally
supportable departure from the familiar, traditional “Basic Services” package in Appendix I of the AIBC
Tariff and carries with that a corresponding, more flexible, sliding scale of recommended fees. It was
developed under the auspices of the AIBC’s Fees and Services Committee, within the Practice Board.
The chief amendments relative to Appendix I’s Basic Services are, broadly: (1) Add: services respecting
one cycle of zoning/development permit applications across the schematic and design development phases;
(2) Delete: bidding and negotiation phase services; (3) Delete: cost estimating in all phases; and (4) Delete:
construction contract administration and payment certification.
Transitional Considerations
Existing client/architect agreements and proposals already submitted are not affected by this bulletin. New
proposals of services-and-fees and new agreements are expected to be in substantial compliance with the
amended Tariff (cf. Bylaw 34.16) by March 08, 2002.

Summary of Approach to the “Market-Multiple Residential Sector” Tariff
These results stem from the research and findings of a working group (representing 14 architectural firms)
that met over the past two years with the objective of updating the Tariff of Fees for Architectural Services
for new construction in the Market Multiple Residential Sector. Market Multiple Residential renovations
were not considered. The phrase “market” suggests a developer-initiated project not involving public
agency participation. Usually in this sector, the terms of the contractual relationship between the owner
and the builder, who in most cases is (effectively) the same party, are neither disclosed to, nor administered
by the architect. Projects characterized as being non-market, or congregate care, were outside the scope of
this review and its recommendations.
Part of the approach was to develop some empirical data to ascertain what are the current acceptable fees
for services in this sector. Members of the working group prepared proposals for a number of hypothetical
projects based on the number of hours it would take to do the projects. This was a form of cost-check and
the catalyst to clarify the basic assumptions underlying the services provided.
Cross-reference was made to the chart of services (Sequence and Scope) on the last page of the current
Tariff. There are black dots beside some of the services that denote “basic” and therefore are covered by
the Tariff’s percentage-fee recommendations. The origin of this list is the research and development work
of the first (1986) Tariff, monitored and updated since, and kept consistent with standard client-architect
agreements, construction contracts and building regulations. The consensus is that the chart has become
somewhat out of step with what is currently the practice in this sector. The enclosed modified list of Basic
Services was developed and endorsed for this sector.
It is notable that in this sector, contrary to the current standard basic services in the Tariff and NPP Client-
Architect Agreement, Document 6, one cycle of the rezoning and development permit process is commonly
included in basic services. On the other hand, tendering is not usually included, and neither are any
services related to progress certificates or quantification of the value of the work. While it is recognized
that the architect needs to approve changes to the work, and to be aware of relevant communications, the
change order procedure does not necessarily require the organizational framework, in this case, as it does
for other sectors.
A review of construction documents was done and a list of necessary Construction Documents (including
working drawings and specifications) was developed. Since tendering and contract administration are not
included in basic services, the specifications in this sector consist mostly of products, performance
standards, assembly illustrations and schedules to satisfy code compliance (i.e. the so-called “technical”
and quality assurance aspects).
The number of variables to consider in providing services during construction makes it extremely difficult
to be precise about the fees. The reviews generically identified in the current Tariff’s Basic Services chart
were expanded and a sequential checklist of field reviews was prepared.
To translate the estimated hours for our hypothetical sample projects into a fee an hourly rate of $85.00 was
used. This was assumed to be a blended rate. It was noted that the beginning and ending of the project
take more “principal’s” time than do the intermediate phases.
Specific Amendments to the AIBC Tariff of Fees for Architectural Services:
1. Basic Services: Add (as Appendix II) the enclosed Sequence and Scope of Services Chart for Market
Multiple Residential Sector Projects, found on this Bulletin’s last page. (Note: for ease of

comparison, the body of this Bulletin shows both the current Chart 1, and Chart 2 for this sector,
side-by-side in newly matching formats).
2. Net percentage Fee Scale, page 27: Delete Table 9 (A) New Construction Market and replace with
the attached graph for new construction (note the list of assumptions in applying the graph). Delete
Table 9 (A) Renovations Market and replace with N/A. Note that 3.6.5 Renovations to Existing
Buildings (versus New Construction) provides a fair approach to assessing fees for additions and
renovations.
3. To 3.1 Alternate Methods of Establishing Fees: Add the following: “For Services during
Construction - i.e. after Building Permit, for Market Multiple Residential Projects, due to the number
and the potential impact of the variables on the scope of services and the number and duration of
field trips, it is recommended that these services be performed a time-basis (see 3.4), hourly or per
diem. The Tariff should be used as a budget reference. It should be kept in mind that the timing and
frequency of field reviews must be at the discretion of the architect. It would be prudent for the
architect and the client to preview the type of field observations the architect must make. If the
extent of field services exceeds what was anticipated, the architect should advise the client of this at
an early stage to ensure proper services and to avoid conflicts regarding fees.” (Notwithstanding the
above, the percentage-fee scales do account for reasonably anticipated construction-phase services.)
4. To 3.2 Allocation of Total Basic Fee to Phases of Service: Add the following: “For Multiple
Residential projects: Services for Schematic and Design Development phases together constitute
about 40 to 45% of the fee and Contract Documentation constitutes about 40 to 45% of the fee. The
fees for Services During Construction would range from 10 to 20% of the fee.”
5. Amend 3.5.1 Operating Assumptions by adding: “For Market Multiple Residential projects refer to
the Sequence and Scope of Services for Market Multiple Residential Projects in the corresponding
Appendix II.”

indicates structural areas of 1,150 m2 of concrete at L1, and 5,000 m2 of wood framing, including roofs and balconies. We
have reviewed Ryzuk geotechnical report and understand conventional spread footings will be appropriate. We understand
that dHk will be the project architect moving forward, and that the project will remain with one level of underground
parking, and the main floor will generally align with above except for some minor structural offsets for small CRU spaces.
The 70 staff at RJC Vancouver Island have significant recent experience with building types similar to those planned for the

mutual respect and good communication amongst the design and construction team leads to successful projects.

Dear Mat,
Re: Proposal for Landscape Architectural Services (Revised),
861-865 Esquimalt Road
Esquimalt, BC
Thank you for inviting LADR to submit a revised proposal for the proposed 6-storey multi-family rental
development located at 861-865 Esquimalt Road in Esquimalt, BC. LADR had previously prepared a fee
proposal in 2021, which is now being updated to reflect our 2024 hourly fees as well as new municipal
requirements related to DP and BP submissions. We recognize that there is now a planned utility ROW
located within the west setback.
We recognize that the current proposal is for a 6-storey multifamily building, with a combination of
surface parking and an underground parkade structure. On-site planting will mostly be located off-slab,
as the parkade structure is generally located within the building footprint and under the surface parking
area. This will allow for trees to have a significant quantity of available soil volume, improving their long-
term health and success. The primary usable outdoor amenity space for the building is the patio at the
southwest corner – this area will feature on-slab planting located in freestanding planters. The main
entry off of Esquimalt Road will feature decorative paving elements and will form a coherent design
along with the required municipal frontage improvements.
This fee proposal is for Landscape Architectural services related to Rezoning, Development Permit,
Building Permit, Tender, Construction Documentation, and Construction Administration. It is based on
the architectural package issued to us January 10, 2024.
Scope of Landscape Architectural Services:
A. Landscape Concept Design for Rezoning & Development Permit
• Startup meeting to confirm the design program and budget with the Client and the architect.
• Create base plans for landscape architectural work.
• Prepare schematic design drawings of proposed development for review with Client and architect
(web based or email).
• Incorporating feedback from reviews, prepare a landscape layout plan and planting plan for
Rezoning submission. Drawings will indicate landscape layout (including areas of lawn, planting
beds, and hardscape); proposed plant species, quantities, and nursery pot size; existing and
proposed tree locations; proposed locations of landscape fencing or screening; and size and
location of usable open space areas.

• The drawing package will include illustrative sections/details and reference images as necessary
to ensure the full design intent is conveyed. As with all LADR’s work, sense of place, CPTED
principles, sustainability and climate adaptation and stormwater management strategies will be
incorporated into the design as feasible.
• Review the concept design with the consultants and Client (web-based or email). Make final
refinements as necessary for Development Permit Application submission.
• Prepare a landscape budget estimate for bonding purposes. NOTE: This is not a construction
estimate.
• 5 web-based meetings and ongoing correspondence (phone and email) with the Client, architect,
other consultants, and municipal staff is allowed for.
• 2 presentations and associated preparation time have been allowed for (Design Panel + Council)
• If additional meetings or other presentations are required, they will be billed on an hourly basis.
NOTE: Phone calls over 30 minutes in length are considered meetings.
• NOTE: No green roofs or rooftop amenity spaces have been allowed for in this fee proposal, and
services related to their design and implementation will be billed on an hourly basis.
• NOTE: If revisions at the Rezoning and/or DP stage are required that exceed the standard
amount allowed for in this fee proposal (moderate revisions related to ongoing consultant
coordination), LADR will provide an estimate for additional fees and a maximum upset price
related to that work.
Fee for Services Related to Landscape Concept Design, Rezoning, and DP: $7,250.00 + GST
B. Building Permit, Tender & Construction Documentation
• NOTE: We expect and have based our fee on the assumption that our approved DP landscape
design will be the foundation for our BP, Tender, and Construction documents. If the submitted
DP design cannot serve as the foundation for construction documents due to changes beyond
LADR’s control, time spent redesigning and updating our CAD file will be billed on an hourly
basis.
• Advance the landscape drawings to create a set of landscape construction documents suitable
for Building Permit & Tender. This includes preparation of a fully dimensioned layout and
materials plan, tree management plan, fully annotated planting plan(s), irrigation sleeving plan,
landscape details, a nursery schedule and a landscape specification including growing medium,
nursery stock and planting requirements, requirements for tree and/or critical root zone
protection during construction, grading plan (if required, for soft landscape areas only), and any
revisions required to coordinate the landscape drawings with engineering drawings.
• Structural construction requirements to be provided by a Structural Engineer. Electrical
construction/connection requirements to be provided by an Electrical Engineer. Paving and
infrastructure requirements to be provided by a Civil Engineer.
• Issue the Tender drawings to the client for final review prior to issuance. An internal Q+A review
will be carried out before issuing to the client.
• Completion of the landscape specification for Tender.
• Respond to bidder queries and prepare Addendums as may be required during the Tender
period.

• Review of plant substitution requests and follow-up recommendations and correspondence
during the tender period.
• 3 web-based consultant meetings have been allowed for during the Building Permit and Tender
phase. Additional meetings will be billed on an hourly basis.
• Ongoing coordination with the client during Tender is allowed for. NOTE: phone calls over 30
minutes in length constitute a meeting and will be billed on an hourly basis.
• Not included in this proposal: A full irrigation plan with specified system components; it is
assumed irrigation will be provided on a design/build basis by an irrigation contractor. If desired,
an irrigation plan and components list can be provided on a disbursement basis with a 10% fee
for coordination. LADR does not have an IIABC Certified irrigation designer in house.
Fee for Services Related to BP, Tender & Construction Documentation: $6,600.00 + GST
C. Construction Contract Administration:
• Prepare IFC drawings, incorporating any addendums, as necessary.
• Review soil reports and prepare amendment and fertilizer recommendations, as necessary.
• Review plant substitution requests with the contractor, nursery staff, and client, as necessary.
• Preparation of CCN’s, CO’s and SI’s as may be required.
• 3 in-person landscape installation reviews are allowed for, including an independent nursery
stock review conducted on-site after the delivery of plant material but before installation
occurs. NOTE: Attendance at site meetings and additional reviews is not included, and if required
will be billed on an hourly basis.
• Ongoing coordination with the client, other consultants, and contractors is allowed for.
• 1 Final Acceptance inspection (as required by Esquimalt and occurring one year after the
issuance of Substantial Completion), as well as accompanying documentation, has been allowed
for. NOTE: If multiple Final Acceptance reviews are required, they will be billed on an hourly
basis.
• NOTE: As-built irrigation drawings to be provided by the irrigation contractor. A landscape
management report is not included in this proposal but can be provided for additional cost if
desired.
Fee for Services Related to Construction Contract Administration: $5,250.00 + GST
Total Fee for Landscape Architectural Services (A+B+C): $19,100.00 + GST
This fee assumes that:
• Any municipally required DP or BP amendment submissions will be billed on an hourly basis. Any
DP or BP resubmissions which are required due to changes made by other consultants, or due to
design changes requested by the applicant will be billed on an hourly basis.
• LADR will not be responsible for preparing details or contract documentation, in part or in
whole, that is normally understood to be the responsibility of the architect, structural, electrical,
mechanical, geotechnical, or civil engineers, or other specialty consultants.

• LADR will not sign or seal any documents that do not solely represent their work, unless the
document also bears the signature and seal of all parties whose work is represented.
• BuiltGreen, LEED or similar sustainability or green rating documentation is not allowed for at
this time.
• LADR will not provide construction estimates.
Disbursements will be charged to the client at cost; vehicle mileage over 5km will be charged at the
current CRA Mileage rate. The 2020 CRA Mileage Rate is $0.59/km for the first 5000 km driven, and
$0.53/km per km for each additional km. Invoices are issued each month and are payable within 30
days. Invoices outstanding after 60 days are subject to 2% interest, added monthly. In the event of
nonpayment LADR reserves the right to suspend work, and, in instances of prolonged nonpayment,
terminate the contract.
This fee proposal is valid for 21 days.
Additional Services
Any services requested by the client or their representatives that are not outlined in the above scope of
work, &/or design changes that result in significant revision work for LADR and are due to Owner
Change, Design Change by Others (not LADR), or Vendor Change or Error, will be considered an

3% per year commencing two years after the contract start date.

It is understood that the project consists of a six story residential development at 861 Esquimalt Road, in
Victoria BC. Approximately 33,620sqft is proposed with two and a half levels of at grade and underground
parking. There are two potential CRU shells proposed along with typical floor plans of 1, 2, and 3 bedroom
suites.
The desired systems are understood to be central heat pumps for heating/cooling, and domestic hot water
with in-suite fan coils and ERV’s as well as a rooftop MUA for building pressurization. There is the potential
for electric DHW generation and central ERV’s, which will be determined during schematic design. The
sustainability target is BC Energy Step Code 3.
It is further understood that a high degree of BIM coordination and integrated design is required with attention
to cost efficiency. Maintenance strategies such as corridor access to in suite fan coils is desired in order to
minimize the need for fire/smoke dampers.

BACKGROUND
The proposed project in Victoria is comprised of Esquimalt consists of a six-storey, wood frame
residential rental building of approx. 33,955 SF with approx. 59 units and a 1.5 level
underground parkade. Units will have balconies.
The envelope assemblies are not clear from the drawings, we assume the exterior walls will be
clad with a conventional cladding system. Glazing systems will be a residential assembly.
Below grade conditions are not confirmed but considering the neighbouring properties we
have assumed that there will be no hydrostatic pressure.
The Municipality of Esquimalt requires Energy Step Code 3 for the building. Our proposal
addresses energy modelling and energy consulting services for Step Code and BCBC. No
additional sustainability measures are being sought. The overarching goal is to have an
efficient building with durable materials.

SCOPE OF SERVICES
BUILDING ENVELOPE SERVICES
We propose to follow the EGBC’s Building Enclosure Practice Guideline for enhanced building
envelope services and we will provide design review and field review for the continuity of the
air barrier (BCBC 5.4), the integrity of the vapour barrier (BCBC 5.5) and moisture barrier (BCBC
5.6) separating the exterior environment from the interior conditioned spaces. The envelope,
for the purpose of this proposal, includes the at-grade waterproofing, opaque walls,
fenestration, roofs, balconies and the transitions between those.

COMPANY PROFILE
Evoke is a building science and energy consulting firm that takes a collaborative approach to
problem solving and keeps client and project goals top of mind. Evoke is a partnership
between dedicated individuals, committed to client satisfaction by providing innovative and
sensible solutions to ever evolving expectations for the built environment.
Expertise that looks to the past and the future
Our experience goes back to the leaky condo crisis and our accumulated knowledge reflects
that. Since then, the industry has changed significantly, addressing durability concerns and
now energy, carbon, and thermal performance are often a central part of project
requirements. We have been part of driving that change. Our goal is to stay ahead of the
curve of what is happening in the industry and to bring our clients leading-edge technical
knowledge while remaining practical with our solutions.
People you can count on
We pride ourselves in building long term
relationships with our clients. Part of our
success resides in our responsiveness and
common sense. Being a smaller company
allows us to be flexible and agile as we are
not constrained by larger organizational
processes. We are also dedicated to
committing the right amount of senior time
to every project and plan to bring the right
people on board as we grow.
Collaboration
One person does not make a team! We know that, and it is in part why we collaborate both
internally and externally to come up with solutions meeting the project’s needs. We are
responsive and address every project in a timely manner; long term relationships are built one
request at a time and this is why we are always ready to help. We are an engaged team that
looks to build a better future, and that starts with your project.
Capacity
Evoke was established in 2020 and has grown from the initial three personnel to our current 19
with offices in Burnaby and Victoria. We currently have two senior building envelope
specialists with considerable experience who provide back up for each other as well as
technical guidance to the team. We have sufficient field staff to meet our current obligations
and are actively hiring to meet future construction schedules as projects come on board.

suite detailing such as baseboards and door trims, windowsills and flooring transitions.

Lighting, Interior Finishes, Bathroom Accessories, Interior Glazing, Interior Doors, Window Coverings, Interior Trims
and Moldings, Appliances and Plumbing Fixtures specifications.
Please note that a standard outline specification document will be produced. This scope of work does not include a
full Master Spec formal specification document. If such a document is required, it will be at an additional expense,
and contracted out to a professional specification writer.

The site currently supports one multi-family dwelling (Lot 861) and one single-family dwelling (Lot

property for on-site parking and outbuildings. Apart from the modest front yard setbacks, land cover for
both lots is largely impervious. The terrain of each lot slopes gently down from Esquimalt Road toward
the rear property boundaries.
TREE RESOURCE
Fifteen trees grow within or immediately adjacent to the proposed development site (see attached
Tree Management Plan drawing).
• Three healthy street trees (all magnolias, tags M-1 through M-3) are situated on the boulevard
fronting the lots between the curb and the sidewalk.
• Two on-site trees, two of which are bylaw-protected, grow on-site:

at the base of the existing retaining wall. This tree exhibits good vigour but poor
structure typical of unmanaged multi-stem examples of this species.
▪ One bylaw-protected White spruce (Tag TR-1216) is in the north-east corner of Lot-865.

along the east boundary of Lot 861. These trees are located atop a 0.75 m- high

damage to one of the two paved driveways accessing the back of Lot 861. There is also
significant aerial encroachment of the crowns of these trees into Lot 861.

structure are located on the two residential lots abutting the south boundary of the site.

DISCUSSION, CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
ANTICIPATED TREE REMOVALS AND MITIGATION MEASURES
Construction of the new six-plex building will result in the loss of 6 protected trees: the four
protected Leyland cypress trees in the group of five growing along the property boundary with
the neighbour to the east, and three of four municipal boulevard trees fronting the site and in the
median of Esquimalt Road.
Leyland cypress “boundary” trees:
Large surficial roots from the Leyland cypress trees are cracking and heaving the adjacent
asphalt driveway access into existing Lot 861. The crowns of the trees extend well into the
proposed building footprint and are not amenable to crown reduction pruning of the magnitude
required. The distance from the base of the trees to the edge of the building excavation,
assuming vertical shoring, is only 1.6 m, which is inside of the critical root plate radius and close
to the zone of rapid root taper. Excavation this close to the trees will destabilize the trees, with
the likelihood of failure and impact very likely with consequences ranging from significant to
severe, depending upon which of several high-value targets are struck.
2 
For these reasons, all
five of these trees are recommended for removal and replacement.
A tree growing across property boundaries is considered in law to be “held in common” between
the two property owners; as such, the consent of both owners is required if the removal of a
boundary tree is desired. Prior to rezoning or a development permit being granted, the
Township of Esquimalt will require written authorization from the co-owner of the Leyland
cypress trees for their removal. Further, the Township’s tree bylaw requires that replacement
trees be planted on the same property from which the associated trees were removed. In this
instance, nine replacement trees are required to mitigate the loss of the four protected cypress
specimens, but it is unclear on which property the replacement trees should be planted.
Assuming permission for the tree removals is obtained, it is recommended that the replacement
trees be divided more or less evenly between the two properties.
Municipal trees:
Road frontage improvements and site servicing will necessitate the removal of two municipal
trees (M-1 and M-4): one magnolia growing on the fronting boulevard that conflicts with the
proposed parkade entrance and one maple growing in the street median that conflicts with
changes to the traffic pattern associated with the development.
RETAINED TREES AND PROTECTION MEASURES
Two municipal boulevard tree (M-1) is proposed for retention and protection. Arborist
supervision shall be provided for all frontage works undertaken by the applicant within or
adjacent to the protected root zone of this tree. Tree protection fencing and caution -
signage shall be erected to the satisfaction of the Township, as indicated on the attached
plan, prior to site work commencing.

Page 7 of 11
All but one of the remaining trees to be preserved are located on the two adjoining lots to
the south of the site. These include two mature Garry oaks (OS-7 and 8), which are located
a safe distance back from the boundary, and two established Western Red cedars (OS-5
and 6) and a small Flowering cherry (OS-4). A small plum (TR-9) located at the south-west
corner of the site. These latter four trees all grow very close to a concrete retaining wall
that divides the proposed development site from the two adjoining properties. The wall
manages a grade change up to the site of approximately 1.5 m measured at the intersection
of the three property boundaries. If this retaining wall has been properly constructed with a
footing on a competent subgrade, there is a good chance that it will have prevented any
migration of tree roots into the proposed site. If this supposition holds true, it will
dramatically reduce any potential impacts arising from the proposed development to these
trees. For this reason, the project intends to maintain and protect this retaining wall in situ
if possible. To this end, it is recommended that the existing grade north of the wall be
maintained or restored once the parkade wall has been constructed (see below).
Tree protection fencing and caution-signage will be emplaced to prevent any encroachment
into the sensitive area between the proposed south parkade wall and the existing retaining
wall without the presence of the project arborist.
Excavation for the parkade along the south side shall be supervised by the project arborist.
In addition to the above, at the recommendation of the project arborist, the south parkade
wall has been shifted north by 1.3 m away from the wall and trees. Care is required to
safely excavate the foundation of the parkade along this wall, while minimizing
encroachment toward the retaining wall. The depth of soil to bedrock is considered to be 3
– 4 m at the south end of the site. Backsloping will be required to safely attack the bedrock
beneath. Shotcrete and soil nailing may also be required. The bedrock will be line-drilled.
Alternate rock removal techniques will be employed where possible . Where blasting is
required, best practices will be deployed to minimize impacts to the existing retaining wall
that the off-site trees adjacent to it, including the following:
• A pre-construction meeting between the general contractor, rock removal contractor
and the project arborist to develop a least-impactful rock removal work plan;
• Line-drilling to minimize overbreakage,
• Use of dynamite in place of ammonium nitrate (less toxic to tree roots) ,
• Creation of a relief zone for the blast wave away from the retaining wall and trees ,
• A drilling and blasting plan that uses smaller charges and minimizes peak particle
velocity,
• “Decking” of explosive charges to sequence the demolition of the charge,
• Deployment of seismometers to measure and record peak particle velocity along
the sensitive areas.
Additional tree protection measures to limit impact related to demolition, site preparation,
construction and landscaping include the following:
• Pre-demolition and construction meetings: Prior to the release of a demolition or building
permit by the City, the applicant and the applicant’s general contractor are required to meet

Page 8 of 11
on site with the project arborist to review the Tree Preservation Plan in detail. The purpose of
the meeting is to systematically review the objectives of the plan and the measures required
to protect trees designated for retention during the demolition, site preparation, construction
and landscape phases of the project. Areas for material storage, on-site trades parking (if
any) shall be identified. The tree protection fencing shall be laid out and standards for
fencing and signage confirmed. The meeting also provides an opportunity to address any
logistical constraints and answer questions.
• Tree Protection Fencing: All tree protection areas (TPAs) shall be fenced to prevent soil
compaction, rutting and other forms of disturbance within the PRZ. If more working room
inside the TPAs is required, the project arborist shall be consulted. If the arborist authorizes
fencing to be altered in order to facilitate more working room, the exposed portion of the root
zone (now) outside the fencing must be protected to prevent soil disturbance. Acceptable
soil-protection materials include steel plates or 200mm of compacted road base on top of
geo-textile cloth or two overlapping layers of ¾” plywood.
• On-site Supervision: All excavation, trenching or rock removal (including blasting) within or
adjacent to TPAs shall be supervised by the project arborist, including trenching for both
municipal service connections and extension of these underground services to the house.
Where considered necessary by the arborist, hand-digging and pneumatic or hydraulic
excavation techniques shall be used in place of mechanical excavation.
• Tree Pruning: The project arborist shall prune any tree roots or branches damaged during
any phase of the project.
• Regular Compliance Monitoring: The project arborist shall develop a schedule of
inspections with the general contractor to resolve emergent tree conflicts, ensure tree
protection fencing remains in place and in good condition and that all applicable tree
protection measures are being observed. Brief field inspection reports shall be provided by
the arborist to the general contractor and the Township’s municipal arborist documenting all
site inspections and on-site work by the project arborist.
• Pre-construction meeting for the landscape phase: Landscaping activities, such as
trenching for irrigation or lighting, grubbing of vegetation, distribution of soils and other
landscape materials – are a significant potential source of damage to the sensitive soils and
root systems of protected trees. Prior to any site preparation or construction activity for
landscaping, the landscape and general contractor shall meet with the project arborist to
review the tree protection plan and measures associated with landscaping.
• The arborist shall supervise all landscape activity within the tree protection areas.
• Post-construction review, remediation of deficiencies and documentation: At
completion of the redevelopment, the arborist shall ensure that any tree protection or
restoration deficiencies are addressed by the owner and building contractor. Once all
deficiencies have been repaired, the arborist shall prepare a letter to the Township of
Esquimalt confirming successful completion of the project, including resolution of any
deficiencies.
Additional detail is provided on the attached tree plan. If diligently implemented, the tree
protection measures specified in the Tree Management Plan and this report will effectively
